n:
- Elkanah was a Levite (a member of the tribe of Levi) ({{1 Chronicles 6:22-27|1 Chronicles 6:22–27}}). After the Israelites conquered the promised land, the Levites received towns in other tribes' territories, including Ephraim ({{Joshua 21:20|Joshua 21:20}}). 

- Elkanah's hometown was Ramah ({{1 Samuel 2:11|1 Samuel 2:11}}). Do not confuse this Ramah with the one in the land of Benjamin (see {{Joshua 18:25|Joshua 18:25}}; {{Judges 19:13|Judges 19:13}}; {{Matthew 2:18|Matthew 2:18}}). 

- The region of Zuph got its name from one of Elkanah's ancestors, a Levite from the Kohath clan ({{1 Chronicles 6:35|1 Chronicles 6:35}}). Saul first met Samuel in Zuph while looking for his father's donkeys ({{1 Samuel 9:5|1 Samuel 9:5}}).

- Elkanah's long family history suggests he was important in society.

Hannah couldn’t have children. In this way she was like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and the mother of Samson.

Her husband Elkanah wasn’t upset about this. But Hannah was only one of Elkanah’s wives. Elkanah’s other wife was named Peninnah. Peninnah was unkind to Hannah because Hannah couldn’t have children.

Hannah was very sad and told God all about her troubles. Her prayer showed how close she was to God. Hannah prayed for God to give her a son. She promised that her son would be set apart as a Nazirite.

Eli spoke a blessing over Hannah. When Samuel was old enough, Hannah kept the promise she had made to God. She took Samuel to Shiloh to live with Eli in the Lord’s house. That was another name for the holy tent.

Hannah’s second prayer was a poem of praise to God. She praised God for rescuing and saving needy people. Her prayer was also a prophecy about a king who would be anointed. She praised God for bringing judgement against evil.

Many years later, Jesus’ mother Mary sang a song to praise God for these same things (Luke 1:46–55).

In the Bible, when a man married two wives at the same time, it often led to serious conflict ({{1 Samuel 1:6-7|1 Samuel 1:6–7}}; {{Genesis 16:1-16|Genesis 16}}; {{Genesis 21:1-34|21}}; {{Genesis 29:1-35|29}}).

- Elkanah made this trip every year because the law required people to attend three festivals a year ({{Exodus 23:14-17|Exodus 23:14–17}}). 

- According to God's law, Israelites had to sacrifice at God's chosen sanctuary ({{Deuteronomy 12:1-28|Deuteronomy 12:1–28}}). From the time of Joshua to Samuel, God's sanctuary, the tabernacle, was in Shiloh ({{Joshua 18:1|Joshua 18:1}}). Shiloh was a town in Ephraim about 13.7 kilometers (8.5 miles) north of Bethel on the way to Shechem. King David later moved the tabernacle to Jerusalem ({{2 Samuel 6:1-23|2 Samuel 6}}). 

- *the LORD of Hosts*: In the Hebrew Old Testament, God is often called *Yahweh Tseba’oth* or *’Elohim Tseba’oth*. These titles are traditionally translated as “Lord of hosts” and “God of hosts.” 

The term “hosts” (Hebrew *tseba’oth*, traditionally “sabaoth”) usually means “armies.” It can refer to human armies, like the armies of Israel (for example, {{1 Samuel 17:45|1 Samuel 17:45}}). I can also refer to foreign armies sent to carry out the Lord’s plans (for example, {{Isaiah 9:11-13|Isaiah 9:11–13}}). However, it most often refers to God's armies of angels sent from heaven to carry out his commands and fight on earth (for example, {{2 Kings 6:17|2 Kings 6:17}}). 

This title highlights God's role as a powerful warrior in the story involving the ark of the covenant and the Philistines ({{1 Samuel 4:1-6:21|1 Samuel 4–6}}).
*Sacrifice … portions [of the meat]*: Some sacrifices included sharing part of the animal in a community meal (see {{Leviticus 7:11-34|Leviticus 7:11–34}}).

*the house of the LORD*: This is another name for the tabernacle. It is also known as “the temple of the LORD” in {{1 Samuel 1:9|1 Samuel 1:9}}. These names show that the tabernacle, a portable building, was the main sanctuary in Shiloh.
*the temple of the LORD*: This means the Lord's sanctuary. Solomon's Temple was not built yet, so *temple* here refers to the Lord's holy place.

Hannah promised to dedicate her child to the Lord as a Nazirite (see {{Numbers 6:1-21|Numbers 6:1–21}}). She might have hoped her child would be like Samson, a deliverer of God's people (compare {{Judges 13:1-25|Judges 13}}). A deliverer was someone who rescued the Israelites from their enemies

Some people may have used the feast times at Shiloh to drink too much alcohol instead of worshiping. Eli wrongly thought Hannah was just another person who was drunk (see {{Acts 2:13-15|Acts 2:13–15}}).

*wicked woman (*Hebrew* a daughter of Belial)*: This phrase describes a worthless person. Belial means "worthlessness" and people later used it as a name for Satan ({{2 Corinthians 6:15|2 Corinthians 6:15}}). In Hebrew, a *son of* or *daughter of* a quality refers to someone who shows that quality strongly.

A blessing was more than just wishful thinking. It was often God's way of giving a real benefit (see, for example, {{Genesis 27:1-40|Genesis 27:1–40}}; {{Genesis 28:1-4|28:1–4}}; {{Genesis 32:22-32|32:22–32}}; {{Genesis 48:1-49:28|48:1–49:28}}). Because this blessing from God's high priest assured Hannah that her prayer would be answered, she was no longer sad.
*After the boy is weaned:* Hannah likely nursed Samuel for two to four years.
Elkanah could have canceled Hannah’s promise (see {{Numbers 30:12-14|Numbers 30:12–14}}). But he chose to affirm and support it instead.

*my horn is exalted*: Literally *has lifted my horn*; see also {{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Samuel 2:10}}. The horn of a strong animal, like an ox or bull, was a symbol of strength. It was raised in victory after defeating an enemy (see also {{1 Kings 22:11|1 Kings 22:11}}).

Hannah’s Prayer of Praise celebrates Samuel's dedication to serving God. It highlights God's: 

- Uniqueness ({{1 Samuel 2:1-2|1 Samuel 2:1–2}})

- Power to change fortunes ({{1 Samuel 2:3-9|1 Samuel 2:3–9}})

- Ability to strengthen his chosen king ({{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Samuel 2:10}})

Like Mary’s Song of Praise in {{Luke 1:46-55|Luke 1:46–55}}, Hannah’s prayer emphasizes God bringing down the rich and powerful and lifting up the poor and oppressed ({{1 Samuel 2:7-8|1 Samuel 2:7–8}}; {{Luke 1:52-53|Luke 1:52–53}}). David’s prayer in {{2 Samuel 22:1-51|2 Samuel 22}} is another beautiful statement of God’s saving power for his chosen king ({{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Samuel 2:10}}). God will bring down the rich, unrighteous rulers (like Eli, Saul, or Herod). Leaders who follow God's will like Samuel, David or Jesus will be lifted up to a higher position or status.

- *no one besides You*: David reacted the same way after hearing God's promises about his kingship ({{2 Samuel 7:22|2 Samuel 7:22}}). 

- *Rock* (compare {{2 Samuel 22:2-3|2 Samuel 22:2–3}}, {{2 Samuel 22:32|32}}): God offers stability and security to those who trust in him.

*Do not boast so proudly, or let arrogance…*: Peninnah showed this attitude (see {{1 Samuel 1:6-7|1 Samuel 1:6–7}}). In contrast, Hannah was humbly dependent on God. This means she did not think too highly of herself. Instead, she trusted in God and relied on him for help.
Hannah celebrated God's power to completely change people's situations.

- Those who were hungry now have enough to eat (see {{1 Samuel 1:7|1 Samuel 1:7}}, {{1 Samuel 1:18|18}}). 

- The phrase *seven children* poetically means that a woman without children would be blessed with a home full of children (see {{1 Samuel 2:21|1 Samuel 2:21}}).

The entire earth belongs to the Lord. God, who created and rules everything, can:

- change circumstances ({{1 Samuel 2:4-8|1 Samuel 2:4–8}}),

- protect those who are faithful ({{1 Samuel 2:9|1 Samuel 2:9}}),

- judge those who are wicked, and

- give strength to his chosen king ({{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Samuel 2:10}}).

- The king was to use his God-given power to help the oppressed, the hungry, and those unable to have children (see {{Psalm 72:1-4|Psalm 72:1 4}}, {{Psalm 72:12-14|12–14}}; {{Proverbs 31:8-9|Proverbs 31:8–9}}). 

- *He will exalt the horn:* See study note on 1 Samuel 2:1.

- *His anointed *(Hebrew *mashiakh*): This part of Hannah’s prayer predicts both Israel’s anointed kings and God’s ultimate Anointed King—the Messiah, Jesus Christ (see {{1 Samuel 12:3-5|1 Samuel 12:3–5}}; {{1 Samuel 24:6|24:6}}, {{1 Samuel 24:10|10}}; {{Psalm 132:17|Psalm 132:17}}; {{Daniel 9:25-26|Daniel 9:25–26}}).

- *wicked men *(Hebrew *sons of Belial*): See study note on 1:16.

- *had no regard for* (literally *did not know*) *the LORD:* Even though they were priests among God's people, they ignored God and did not follow his will (compare {{Jeremiah 2:8|Jeremiah 2:8}}).

Eli’s sons did evil things as priests and Eli didn’t stop them. Samuel acted differently than they did. Samuel wasn’t in the family line of Aaron. But he served God faithfully like priests were supposed to.

The first message that Samuel shared as a prophet was against Eli and his sons. The prophecy came true after a battle between the people of Israel and the Philistines. The Israelites wanted God to protect them and to help them win the battle. They used the ark of the covenant to try and force God to do this. But they weren’t obeying God or trusting him to save them. This was very different from how the ark was used in the battle against Jericho (Joshua 6:1–14).

Eli’s sons were killed in the battle with the Philistines. Eli died when he heard that the Philistines captured the ark of the covenant. The Philistines suffered a plague because they had taken the ark. The plague was God’s judgement against them. It showed them that God was more powerful than their false gods.

When the ark was returned to Israel, Samuel served the Israelites as their leader. He was the last one to lead like the 12 judges had led. He helped the Israelites turn back to God. They stopped worshipping false gods and instead worshipped only God. This showed that they were being faithful to the Mount Sinai covenant. Then God saved them from their enemies. This was one of the covenant blessings.

The priests were meant to take their share of the meat only after it was boiled (see {{Numbers 6:19|Numbers 6:19}}). Eli’s sons ignored God's rules ({{1 Samuel 2:13-14|1 Samuel 2:13–14}}, {{1 Samuel 2:17|17}}).

God's law stated that the fat from a sacrificial animal belonged to the Lord. The priests had to burn the fat on the altar before anything else could be done with the animal ({{Leviticus 3:3-17|Leviticus 3:3–17}}).

- The phrase *Samuel served the Lord* refers to the religious duties of Levites and priests (see, for example, {{Numbers 3:4|Numbers 3:4}}; {{Numbers 8:19|8:19}}, {{Numbers 8:24|24}}; {{Deuteronomy 18:7|Deuteronomy 18:7}}). Samuel, like Eli's sons, was a Levite (see study note on 1 Samuel 1:1). However, unlike Eli's sons, Samuel performed his duties well.

- He wore a linen garment similar to what priests wore when serving in the sanctuary (see study note on 1 Samuel 22:18).

*Eli would bless*: Blessing was one of the functions of a priest ({{Numbers 6:23-27|Numbers 6:23–27}}; {{Deuteronomy 10:8|Deuteronomy 10:8}}; {{1 Chronicles 23:13|1 Chronicles 23:13}}). See study note on 1 Samuel 1:17–18.

- *sleeping with the women*: Eli’s sons were likely influenced by Canaanite religious practices, which included sex as part of the ceremony.

- *who served at the entrance*: See {{Exodus 38:8|Exodus 38:8}}.
Eli's weak efforts to correct his the behavior of his sons (see {{1 Samuel 2:29|1 Samuel 2:29}}) show he raised them without discipline ({{1 Samuel 3:13|1 Samuel 3:13}}).

- *God* (or *the judges*; Hebrew* ’elohim*): The Hebrew word translated *intercede* is plural here. When ’elohim means "God" it often takes a singular verb. Some ancient translations interpret ’*elohim* as “judges” in this context. If so, the judges would mediate for the guilty in a human court. Yet, many Hebrew scholars argue that *’elohim* should not be translated as “judges.” If so, how could God *intercede *for the man who sinned? Eli might have believed that court decisions came directly from God. God might work through his written laws or through other events to either free or find guilty a person accused of doing something wrong. Or Eli might have been talking about the system of animal sacrifices.

- The sexual wrongdoing in ({{1 Samuel 2:22|1 Samuel 2:22}}) and excessive eating in ({{1 Samuel 2:12-17|1 Samuel 2:12–17}}) of Eli’s sons were sins against the Lord. This was because they were corrupting how Israel worshiped God. No one can speak to God on behalf of sinners who completely refuse to follow God's will (see {{Matthew 12:31|Matthew 12:31}}).

- Eli’s sons ignored their father because the Lord had already started to punish them by making their hearts stubborn (see {{Exodus 4:21|Exodus 4:21}}; {{Exodus 7:3|7:3}}; {{Exodus 8:15-32|8:15–32}}; {{Exodus 10:27|10:27}}; {{Exodus 11:10|11:10}}).

As children, both Samuel and Jesus had extraordinary qualities ({{1 Samuel 2:21|1 Samuel 2:21}}; see also {{Luke 2:40|Luke 2:40}}, {{Luke 2:52|52}}). Samuel was one of Jesus' forerunners (someone who came before and prepared the way). Samuel showed what would happen to Jesus through his words, actions, and sometimes through events in his own life that were similar to what would happen in Jesus' life.
"Man of God" is another name for a prophet ({{1 Samuel 9:6|1 Samuel 9:6}}; {{1 Kings 13:1|1 Kings 13:1}}; {{2 Kings 1:9|2 Kings 1:9}}).
Eli did not stop his sons from doing wrong, showing disrespect for God's sacrifices and offerings. Eli gained from their actions, so God blamed him for allowing it.

*that your house and the house of your father would walk before Me forever*: See {{Exodus 29:9|Exodus 29:9}} and {{Numbers 25:13|Numbers 25:13}}. God will honor another of Aaron’s descendants (see study note on 1 Samuel 2:35) and reject Eli’s family, removing them from the priesthood ({{1 Samuel 2:31-35|1 Samuel 2:31–35}}).

*reach old age*: In the Old Testament, a short life often shows God's disapproval. A long life shows God's blessing (see {{Genesis 15:15|Genesis 15:15}}; {{1 Kings 3:14|1 Kings 3:14}}; {{Psalm 91:16|Psalm 91:16}}).
*a faithful priest*: Zadok and his family later took over the priesthood from Eli's family ({{1 Kings 2:26-27|1 Kings 2:26–27}}, {{1 Kings 2:35|35}}).

*the word of the LORD was rare, and visions were scarce*: God was not revealing his will through prophets or priests. This means that God was not regularly speaking to his people or giving them guidance.

However, this time of spiritual darkness was about to end when God began to communicate with Samuel ({{1 Samuel 3:2-4:1|1 Samuel 3:2–4:1a}}).
Eli could barely see, both with his eyes and in his faith ({{1 Samuel 3:1|1 Samuel 3:1}}).

- The priests had to keep God's lamp burning all night ({{Exodus 27:20-21|Exodus 27:20–21}}; {{Exodus 30:7-8|30:7–8}}). 

- Samuel sleeping near the ark shows his closeness to God's presence and purpose, unlike Eli and his sons.

*Samuel did not yet know the LORD*: This was because he had no direct experience with the Lord. In contrast, Eli's sons did not know the Lord because they were morally and spiritually lacking (see study note on 1 Samuel 2:12).
*Eli realized:* Even with his flaws, Eli still had some spiritual insight.

- Repeating the name highlights the importance of the moment (see {{Genesis 22:11|Genesis 22:11}}; {{Exodus 3:4|Exodus 3:4}}; {{Matthew 27:46|Matthew 27:46}}; {{Luke 22:31|Luke 22:31}}; {{Acts 9:4|Acts 9:4}}). 

- Samuel leaves out “Lord” (see {{1 Samuel 3:9|1 Samuel 3:9}}) in his reply, possibly out of respect for the name or because he was unsure who was speaking.

*something in Israel at which the ears of all who hear it will tingle*: This phrase shows how serious God's judgment is. God's actions would also have a major impact on Israel as a nation (see {{2 Kings 21:12|2 Kings 21:12}}; {{Jeremiah 19:3|Jeremiah 19:3}}).
*Everything I have spoken*: See {{1 Samuel 2:27-36|1 Samuel 2:27–36}}.

- *because his sons blasphemed God*: They showed contempt for God through their actions.

- *he did not restrain them*: Eli scolded his sons ({{1 Samuel 2:23-25|1 Samuel 2:23–25}}), but he did not stop them.

Blood sacrifices and offerings would not be accepted for Eli and his sons. The offerings in {{Leviticus 4:1-5:19|Leviticus 4–5}} were for accidental or unintentional sins. But Eli and his sons sinned on purpose and rebelliously.
Samuel was scared to tell Eli about God's plans for him and his family. He either respected Eli's position or feared for his own safety.
*He let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground*: Samuel was a true prophet, as shown in {{1 Samuel 3:20|1 Samuel 3:20}} and {{Deuteronomy 18:21-22|Deuteronomy 18:21–22}}.

- The entire nation, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, recognized Samuel as God's prophet. 

- *confirmed as a prophet*: Samuel's reliable messages ({{1 Samuel 3:19|1 Samuel 3:19}}) showed that God spoke through him.

- *the LORD continued to appear*: God started talking to Israel again through Samuel (see {{1 Samuel 3:1|1 Samuel 3:1}}).

- *Shiloh*: Refer to study note on 1 Samuel 1:3.

- *the Philistines*: See “The Philistines” Profile.

- The exact location of Ebenezer is unknown. It was likely just east of Aphek (see also {{1 Samuel 7:12|1 Samuel 7:12}} and 1 Samuel 7:12). 

- Aphek was west of Shiloh, far inland and north of Philistine territory. By camping there, the Philistines might have been trying to take more Israelite land.
The crisis with the ark of the covenant showed Israel needed Samuel's leadership. It also fulfilled prophecies about Eli and his sons ({{1 Samuel 3:11-14|1 Samuel 3:11–14}}).

The Israelites were often defeated in war because of the sin of one individual or the entire nation ({{Joshua 7:1-26|Joshua 7}}). In this defeat, no one checked if sin was the reason. It seems no one asked the Lord if they should fight the Philistines in the first place (see {{1 Chronicles 14:13-16|1 Chronicles 14:13–16}}). Instead, the Israelites used the ark, the most sacred symbol of the Lord’s presence, as a way to bring good luck. Bringing the ark into battle was not always wrong (see {{Joshua 6:2-21|Joshua 6:2–21}}), but it did not guarantee God’s blessing and victory.

- *the LORD of Hosts*: See study note on 1 Samuel 1:3. 

- *enthroned between the cherubim*: This represents God's glorious presence above the ark in the Most Holy Place (God’s “throne room”). 

- Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, being involved signals the disaster to come (see {{1 Samuel 3:11-14|1 Samuel 3:11–14}}).
Like the Israelites, the Philistines saw the ark as a powerful charm (see {{1 Samuel 4:2-3|1 Samuel 4:2–3}}). They believed it would lead to their defeat in battle.

- *the gods who struck the Egyptians*: The Philistines, who worshiped many gods, knew about the Lord’s power. However, they did not understand that he was the one true God. 

- *Struck … with all kinds of plagues*: The Lord later demonstrated his power against the Philistines in a similar way (see {{1 Samuel 5:6|1 Samuel 5:6–6:6}}).
30,000 was over seven times the number who had died before without the ark ({{1 Samuel 4:2|1 Samuel 4:2}}). The Israelites learned that the ark was not a magical object to prevent bad luck.

- The capture of the ark was a huge blow to the Israelites ({{1 Samuel 4:12-22|1 Samuel 4:12–22}}).

- The deaths of Hophni and Phinehas fulfilled God's promise to Eli ({{1 Samuel 2:34|1 Samuel 2:34}}). Although they are the only ones mentioned, other Israelites had also sinned (see {{1 Samuel 7:3-6|1 Samuel 7:3–6}}).
*his clothes torn and dirt on his head*: This shows grief and loss (for example, {{Joshua 7:6|Joshua 7:6}}; {{2 Samuel 1:2|2 Samuel 1:2}}; {{2 Samuel 15:32|15:32}}; {{Job 2:12|Job 2:12}}).
*could not see*: See {{1 Samuel 3:2|1 Samuel 3:2}} and study note on 1 Samuel 3:2.

- *Eli fell backward*: This was possibly from shock or a heart attack when he heard the message. His deadly fall represents his family's loss of the priesthood and the end of the wrongdoing his sons started ({{1 Samuel 2:12-17|1 Samuel 2:12–17}}). 

- *Eli had judged Israel*: Being a priest and a judge was possible at the same time (compare {{Exodus 18:13-26|Exodus 18:13–26}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:8-13|Deuteronomy 17:8–13}}). Samuel took over as Israel’s judge and provided the leadership Eli did not (see {{1 Samuel 7:12-17|1 Samuel 7:12–17}}).

- The phrase *forty years* connects Eli’s career to the timeline and themes of the book of Judges (compare {{Judges 3:11|Judges 3:11}}; {{Judges 5:31|5:31}}; {{Judges 8:28|8:28}}; {{Judges 13:1|13:1}}).

The name *Ichabod* includes the Hebrew word *kabod*, meaning glory (see {{Exodus 24:15-17|Exodus 24:15–17}}). A similar word describes Eli in {{1 Samuel 4:18|1 Samuel 4:18}} (Hebrew *kabed*, meaning heavy). The ark's disappearance mirrors the fall of Eli’s family. The Israelites lost divine glory and protection (compare {{Ezekiel 8:1-10:22|Ezekiel 8–10}}; {{Luke 19:41-44|Luke 19:41–44}}; {{Luke 21:20-24|21:20–24}}), but God's glorious presence would later return to them ({{1 Samuel 6:1-21|1 Samuel 6:1–21}}; compare {{Ezekiel 43:1-8|Ezekiel 43:1–8}}).

- *Ebenezer*: See study note on 1 Samuel 4:1b. 

- Ashdod* was *one of the five main Philistine cities (see {{1 Samuel 6:17|1 Samuel 6:17}}). It was on the same major trade route (the Great Trunk Road) as Aphek.

Dagon was a god worshipped by the Philistines (see {{Judges 16:23-24|Judges 16:23–24}}). The name might come from the Hebrew word *dag*, which means "fish." This would be an appropriate name for a god of seafaring people. However, it is more likely related to the Hebrew word *dagan*, which means "grain." This would indicate a god of fertility or agriculture.
*his head and his hands broken off*: This was a symbol of God's power over the idol ({{1 Samuel 5:7|1 Samuel 5:7}}; see also {{1 Samuel 17:51|17:51}}).

*step on the threshold*: The Philistines might have thought Dagon's statue broke because they did not honor him correctly. However, their real mistake was worshiping an idol instead of the one true God ({{Isaiah 44:6-20|Isaiah 44:6–20}}).

*tumors*: The Hebrew word might just mean "swellings." Another possible translation is "hemorrhoids." They could have been deadly *buboes* from the bubonic plague, affecting the lower body, especially the rectal area. Rats are known to carry the plague.

- *rulers *(or *overlords*): Each of the five major Philistine cities had its own ruler ({{1 Samuel 6:16-18|1 Samuel 6:16–18}}).

- *It must be moved*: Even with the clear danger, the Philistines valued their captured trophy so much that they chose to move it instead of returning it. 

- Gath, one of the five major Philistine cities, was close by.

God often caused great panic to disable and overpower Israel's enemies ({{1 Samuel 14:15|1 Samuel 14:15}}, {{1 Samuel 14:20|20}}; {{Deuteronomy 7:23|Deuteronomy 7:23}}; {{Ezekiel 22:5|Ezekiel 22:5}}; {{Amos 3:9|Amos 3:9}}).
Ekron, one of the five main Philistine cities (see {{1 Samuel 6:17|1 Samuel 6:17}}), was only five miles north of Gath.
*priests and diviners*: Fortune telling was part of the Philistine religion (see {{1 Samuel 28:7|1 Samuel 28:7}}; {{Deuteronomy 18:10-14|Deuteronomy 18:10–14}}).

The Philistines probably did not know about Israelite worship rules. A Philistine guilt offering was likely a payment to their god. It was to avoid his anger. This differs from the idea of atonement in {{Leviticus 16:1-34|Leviticus 16}}.
The Philistines believed they could defeat the Lord by fighting harder ({{1 Samuel 4:9|1 Samuel 4:9}}). They had beaten the Israelites, but now understood they could not defeat Israel's God.

*take their calves away*: If the cows ignored their motherly instincts and left their calves to take the Ark to Israel, it would show that the plague came from Israel's God ({{1 Samuel 6:9|1 Samuel 6:9}}).
Beth-shemesh was the nearest Israelite town to Ekron (a Philistine city) ({{1 Samuel 5:10|1 Samuel 5:10}}).
People usually harvested wheat in May or June (late spring or early summer).

This burnt offering might have been for forgiveness of sin (see {{1 Samuel 7:9-10|1 Samuel 7:9–10}}; {{Leviticus 1:3-17|Leviticus 1:3–17}}). But, it was more likely a voluntary act of love or gratitude (see {{Leviticus 22:18-22|Leviticus 22:18–22}}).

Fortunately, the ark arrived in Beth-shemesh ({{1 Samuel 6:13|1 Samuel 6:13}}), a city of the Levites ({{Joshua 21:13-16|Joshua 21:13–16}}). The Levite men living there could safely move the ark (see {{Numbers 4:15|Numbers 4:15}}).

- *guilt offering*: See study note on 1 Samuel 6:3.

- *Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron*: These were the five main Philistine cities. They were on or near the Great Trunk Road, an important ancient trade route. This route connected Egypt with Mesopotamia through the coastal plain of Canaan. Each city had a ruler similar to a king ({{1 Samuel 6:16|1 Samuel 6:16}}).

- *seventy men*: Beth-shemesh was a small village. 

- *because they looked inside the ark*: Touching the ark was not allowed ({{Numbers 4:15|Numbers 4:15}}; {{2 Samuel 6:6-8|2 Samuel 6:6–8}}), as was looking inside it ({{Numbers 4:20|Numbers 4:20}}). The men who died did not respect God's holiness.

- *Who can stand*: Even God's people faced his wrath when they disrespected his holiness. The wrath of God is God's strong disapproval of human beings and their sinful actions.

- *To whom should the ark go up from here?:* When confronted with God's holiness, the Israelites felt the same distress as the pagan Philistines ({{1 Samuel 6:2|1 Samuel 6:2}}).
Kiriath-jearim was close, about 16 kilometers (10 miles) northeast of Beth-shemesh.

- The men of Kiriath-jearim who moved the ark and Eleazar were likely Levites (see {{1 Samuel 6:15|1 Samuel 6:15}}; {{Numbers 1:47-51|Numbers 1:47–51}}).

- *to guard the ark*: The same verb describes the Levites’ duty to guard the tabernacle ({{Numbers 1:53|Numbers 1:53}}; {{Numbers 3:7|3:7}}).
Twenty years passed until Samuel gathered the people at Mizpah ({{1 Samuel 7:5-6|1 Samuel 7:5–6}}). Later, David moved the ark to Jerusalem ({{2 Samuel 6:1-19|2 Samuel 6:1–19}}).

- People cannot expect God's blessing unless they remove what goes against his will (see {{Genesis 35:2|Genesis 35:2}}; {{Joshua 24:14|Joshua 24:14}}). 

- Ashtoreth was the Canaanite goddess of fertility linked to Baal ({{1 Samuel 7:4|1 Samuel 7:4}}). Worshiping Canaanite gods was a constant issue in Israel's history. The people began idol worship during the twenty years in {{1 Samuel 7:2|1 Samuel 7:2}}. It may have started in the time of the judges ({{1 Samuel 8:8|1 Samuel 8:8}}; {{Judges 6:25|Judges 6:25}}; compare {{Amos 5:25-26|Amos 5:25–26}}). Israel's crushing defeat by the Philistines was not only due to the sins of Eli's two sons but also several generations of unfaithfulness to God.
Israel's victory over the Philistines was due to their improved relationship with God, not because of the ark's presence (see {{1 Samuel 4:3-11|1 Samuel 4:3–11}}).

- Mizpah was a government center and gathering place for the nation (see {{1 Samuel 7:16|1 Samuel 7:16}}; {{1 Samuel 10:17|10:17}}; {{Judges 20:1|Judges 20:1}}). 

- *I will pray … on your behalf*: Eli’s question in {{1 Samuel 2:25|1 Samuel 2:25}} is answered here; Samuel was the mediator Israel needed.

- *drew water … poured it out*: This ceremony is not mentioned elsewhere in the Old Testament. 

- Sometimes, Israelites fasted (did not eat) to show grief or seek the Lord’s favor ({{2 Samuel 1:12|2 Samuel 1:12}}; {{2 Samuel 12:22-23|12:22–23}}; {{1 Kings 21:27|1 Kings 21:27}}; {{Ezra 8:21-23|Ezra 8:21–23}}; {{Nehemiah 9:1|Nehemiah 9:1}}; {{Esther 4:3|Esther 4:3}}, {{Esther 4:16|16}}; {{Joel 2:12|Joel 2:12}}; compare {{Luke 2:37|Luke 2:37}}; {{Acts 13:2-3|Acts 13:2–3}}; {{Acts 14:23|14:23}}). 

- Having Samuel as Israel’s judge was refreshing compared to Eli’s poor leadership (see {{1 Samuel 4:18|1 Samuel 4:18}} and 1 Samuel 4:18) and the leadership of some other judges, for example:

- Gideon ({{Judges 8:22-27|Judges 8:22–27}}) 

- Jephthah ({{Judges 11:30-12:7|Judges 11:30–12:7}})

- Samson ({{Judges 13:1-16:21|Judges 13:1–16:21}})

- The whole burnt offering was likely for forgiveness of sin (see {{Leviticus 1:1-4|Leviticus 1:1–4}}). 

- The Lord responded with a loud thunderclap ({{1 Samuel 7:10|1 Samuel 7:10}}).

*thundered loudly*: See {{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Samuel 2:10}}. God often used thunder to confuse and defeat Israel’s enemies (for example, {{Exodus 14:24|Exodus 14:24}}; {{Exodus 23:27|23:27}}; {{Joshua 10:10|Joshua 10:10}}; {{Judges 4:15|Judges 4:15}}).

*Ebenezer*: We do not know where this stone memorial is located. The Philistines had defeated Israel and taken the ark at a place with the same name ({{1 Samuel 4:1|1 Samuel 4:1}}; {{1 Samuel 5:1|5:1}}). Samuel set up this memorial to honor God's help in reversing the Philistine attacks.

- The Philistines remained inactive for a while, until Saul became king (see {{1 Samuel 13:5|1 Samuel 13:5}}).

- God's powerful intervention, not Samuel's talents, was crucial in freeing Israel from the Philistines.

The Amorites lived in Canaan and the region east of the Jordan River before Israel took over the promised land (see {{Genesis 15:16|Genesis 15:16}}; {{Deuteronomy 3:8|Deuteronomy 3:8}}; {{Joshua 2:10|Joshua 2:10}}). Some Amorites stayed in the region after the conquest (see {{2 Samuel 21:2|2 Samuel 21:2}}).
*judged Israel all the days of his life*: After Saul became king ({{1 Samuel 10:1-27|1 Samuel 10}}), Samuel mainly served as a judge, not a military leader.

- Bethel and Mizpah were places where people gathered during the time of the judges ({{Judges 20:1|Judges 20:1}}, {{Judges 20:18|18}}, {{Judges 20:26|26}}; {{Judges 21:1-2|21:1–2}}). This was the time in Israel’s history after the death of Joshua and before the beginning of the monarchy (when kings ruled). During this time, God raised up judges to lead and deliver Israel. Bethel was important even in Abraham's time ({{Genesis 12:8|Genesis 12:8}}; {{Genesis 13:3-4|13:3–4}}; {{Genesis 28:10-22|28:10–22}}; {{Genesis 35:1-15|35:1–15}}).

- Gilgal, near Jericho, was a holy place since Joshua's time ({{Joshua 4:19-24|Joshua 4:19–24}}; {{Joshua 5:2-10|5:2–10}}). From these places, Samuel guided "all the people of Israel" ({{1 Samuel 10:17|1 Samuel 10:17}}).
Samuel was from Ramah (see {{1 Samuel 1:1|1 Samuel 1:1}}).

Samuel’s sons weren’t faithful to God like Samuel was. The Israelites didn’t want them as leaders. The Israelites no longer wanted to be led by judges. They no longer wanted God to be their only Ruler. Instead, they wanted a human being to be their king.

The people groups around the Israelites were led by kings. The Israelites wanted to be like those people groups. They thought that a human king would solve their problems. The Israelites' problem was that the people groups around them were treating them badly. This was one of the covenant curses.

It happened because the Israelites weren’t faithful to the Mount Sinai covenant. It happened because they didn’t fully drive out the Canaanites. The Israelites thought a human king would help them win battles over those people groups. That is how they hoped to enjoy the covenant blessing of peace.

Winning battles was more important to them than serving God with all their heart. This made Samuel very sad. It also made God very sad. God allowed his people (God’s people) to have a king. Samuel explained clearly how the king should act. Those rules are recorded in Deuteronomy 17:14–20.

Saul started out as a humble king. He was a farmer and was willing to be used by the Holy Spirit. All the Israelites accepted him. They accepted him after he rescued the town of Jabesh Gilead from the king of Ammon.

Samuel made it clear to the Israelites that they had refused to accept God as their King. They were sad that they had done this and recognised that they had sinned. Samuel encouraged them to follow God no matter what happened. The people and the king were to live according to God’s ways.

When Israel was changing to a monarchy (rule by kings), neither God ({{1 Samuel 8:7-9|1 Samuel 8:7–9}}) nor Samuel ({{1 Samuel 12:1-25|1 Samuel 12:1–25}}) liked the people's request for a king. Saul, the first king ({{1 Samuel 9:1-11:15|1 Samuel 9–11}}), did not succeed in his role ({{1 Samuel 13:1-31:13|1 Samuel 13–31}}) and proved Samuel's warnings true (see {{1 Samuel 8:10-18|1 Samuel 8:10–18}}; compare {{1 Samuel 16:1-13|1 Samuel 16:1–13}}).
Samuel’s two oldest sons served as judges in Beersheba, which is 80.5 kilometers (50 miles) south of their father's home.
*his sons did not walk in his ways*: They were more like Eli’s two sons ({{1 Samuel 2:12-17|1 Samuel 2:12–17}}). Their corruption was a main reason the time of the judges ended.

- *you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways*: Judges were usually local leaders. But kings, as national leaders, could unite the entire nation during crises ({{1 Samuel 8:20|1 Samuel 8:20}}). However, a spiritual issue was behind the request for a king ({{1 Samuel 8:7-8|1 Samuel 8:7–8}}). 

- Other nations, like Egypt and Sumer, were ruled by kings for nearly 2,000 years before Samuel’s time.
Samuel was unhappy. He likely felt personally rejected ({{1 Samuel 8:7|1 Samuel 8:7}}).

- *Listen to the voice of the people*: God rarely told a prophet to listen to the misguided people. The people's desires and God's will would align with King David (see {{2 Samuel 7:8-17|2 Samuel 7:8–17}}). 

- *they have rejected Me*: By rejecting judges, they were actually rejecting God's rule and authority (see also {{1 Samuel 12:1-17|1 Samuel 12:1–17}}).

*serving other gods*: The people’s request for a king showed a lack of trust in God. They wanted a human ruler to give them security instead of relying on God as their king. Because of this, Israel’s monarchy was a divine concession (something God allowed), not a divine gift. Any king or human institution becomes idolatrous when people trust it more than they trust God.
These verses explain why being a king has downsides. Each sentence describes something the king would take. A king would seize things, not just protect them.
The people wanted a king to *lead* them, but Samuel warned that the king would control them. They asked for a leader but got a ruler.
The king would take both people and their belongings.

People had to give a tenth of their harvest as a sacred donation to support God's temple and its workers ({{Deuteronomy 12:6|Deuteronomy 12:6}}, {{Deuteronomy 12:17-18|17–18}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:22-29|14:22–29}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:12-15|26:12–15}}). The king also required another tenth, which was a heavy burden due to the unpredictable nature of farming.
*you yourselves will become his slaves*: By asking for a king, the people whose ancestors were once slaves in Egypt risked becoming enslaved again (see {{1 Kings 12:1-20|1 Kings 12:1 20}}).
The people would plead for relief, just like their ancestors did in Egypt under a harsh ruler (see {{Exodus 3:7|Exodus 3:7}}).

- God had set Israel apart from other nations ({{Leviticus 20:26|Leviticus 20:26}}; {{Numbers 23:9|Numbers 23:9}}). By wanting a king and wishing to be like other nations, they were rejecting God's plan (see {{1 Samuel 8:5-7|1 Samuel 8:5–7}}; compare {{Deuteronomy 17:14|Deuteronomy 17:14}}). 

- *to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles.”*: Kings had three main roles:

- waging wars, both offensive and defensive,

- enforcing laws, and

- ensuring economic stability.
*repeated them in the hearing of the LORD*: A prophet's role included presenting the people's concerns to God (see {{Numbers 27:5|Numbers 27:5}}).
*Appoint a king for them*: See study note on 1 Samuel 8:7; compare with {{Romans 1:24-26|Romans 1:24–26}}.
*a powerful man, whose name was Kish:* Saul came from a wealthy family.

Saul became powerful through three main events: 

- Samuel secretly anointed him ({{1 Samuel 9:1-10:16|1 Samuel 9:1–10:16}}).

- He was chosen by casting lots ({{1 Samuel 10:17-27|1 Samuel 10:17–27}}).

- He defeated the Ammonites ({{1 Samuel 11:1-15|1 Samuel 11:1–15}}).

See also study note on 1 Samuel 13:1–16:13.

Saul's looks, *choice and handsome, without equal among the Israelites*, made people loyal to him (see {{1 Samuel 10:23|1 Samuel 10:23}}; compare {{1 Samuel 16:12|16:12}}; {{2 Samuel 14:25-26|2 Samuel 14:25–26}}).
Zuph, likely in Ephraim, was where Samuel came from ({{1 Samuel 1:1|1 Samuel 1:1}}). God guided Saul to this place.
The phrase *man of God* referred to a prophet (see {{1 Samuel 2:27|1 Samuel 2:27}}; also {{Deuteronomy 33:1|Deuteronomy 33:1}}; {{Joshua 14:6|Joshua 14:6}}; {{1 Kings 13:1-32|1 Kings 13:1–32}}).

*no gift to take to the man*: It was common to bring a gift when asking for a prophet's help (see {{1 Kings 14:2-3|1 Kings 14:2–3}}; {{2 Kings 5:5|2 Kings 5:5}}, {{2 Kings 5:15|15}}; {{2 Kings 8:8|8:8}}). Some false prophets asked for gifts in exchange for their services ({{Micah 3:11|Micah 3:11}}). Saul's concern might show a misunderstanding, thinking he could buy advice from a prophet of God ({{Acts 8:20|Acts 8:20}}).

- Community leaders usually met for business at the town gates (see {{Ruth 4:1-2|Ruth 4:1–2}}).

- *have a sacrifice on the high place*: Samuel is one of the few people who combined prophetic and priestly roles (others include Moses, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Jesus).

- *the high place*: An open-air altar or platform on a hill near the city gate. High places often became sites for pagan idolatry (see {{Numbers 33:52|Numbers 33:52}}; {{1 Kings 15:14|1 Kings 15:14}}; {{1 Kings 22:43|22:43}}; {{2 Kings 12:3|2 Kings 12:3}}; {{2 Kings 14:4|14:4}}; {{2 Kings 15:4|15:4}}, {{2 Kings 15:35|35}}).

- *To eat*: During worship, part of a sacrifice was burned on the altar. The rest was eaten in a ceremonial feast by the guests (see also {{1 Samuel 1:4|1 Samuel 1:4}}).

- *To bless the food*: As a Levite, Samuel's role as a priest included offering blessings (see {{Deuteronomy 10:8|Deuteronomy 10:8}}; {{Deuteronomy 21:5|21:5}}).

- God's command to anoint Saul (by pouring olive oil on his head) marked his rise in status and dedication for a special purpose (see {{Exodus 30:22-33|Exodus 30:22–33}}; {{Leviticus 8:12|Leviticus 8:12}}; {{1 Kings 19:16|1 Kings 19:16}}; {{Isaiah 45:1|Isaiah 45:1}}).

- *he will save them*: As they had asked for ({{1 Samuel 8:20|1 Samuel 8:20}}; compare {{Judges 13:5|Judges 13:5}}). David eventually defeated the Philistines ({{2 Samuel 5:17-25|2 Samuel 5:17–25}}; {{2 Samuel 8:1|8:1}}; {{2 Samuel 21:15|21:15}}, {{2 Samuel 21:18-22|18–22}}). 

- *their cry has come to Me* (compare {{Exodus 3:7-9|Exodus 3:7–9}}): The Philistines were again trying to conquer Israel and make them pay tribute as subjects.

- *the smallest tribe*: Saul tried to downplay Benjamin's importance, but they were strong warriors ({{Judges 20:14-31|Judges 20:14–31}}; see study note on 1 Samuel 10:17). What better tribe to lead in battle?

- *least of all the clans*: See {{1 Samuel 9:1|1 Samuel 9:1}}.
A typical house had a flat roof used for many purposes, like sleeping during warm weather (see {{Deuteronomy 22:8|Deuteronomy 22:8}}; {{2 Kings 4:10|2 Kings 4:10}}).

- Samuel did this again by anointing David with olive oil ({{1 Samuel 16:13|1 Samuel 16:13}}).

- The people of Israel belonged to the Lord, not the king. The king was to manage, not own, them (compare {{1 Samuel 8:10-18|1 Samuel 8:10–18}}).
*Rachel's tomb in Zelzah*: See {{Genesis 35:16-20|Genesis 35:16–20}}; the exact location is not known.
These three "signs" were meant to convince a hesitant Saul ({{1 Samuel 9:21|1 Samuel 9:21}}) that he was truly chosen to be king.

- *Oak of Tabor*: This place is in Benjamin and should not be mixed up with the village named Tabor in Zebulun ({{1 Chronicles 6:77|1 Chronicles 6:77}}). 

- *Bethel*: See study note on 1 Samuel 7:16.

- Gibeah of God, Saul’s hometown ({{1 Samuel 10:26|1 Samuel 10:26}}), was once a lawless city ({{Judges 19:1-21:25|Judges 19–21}}). It is not described elsewhere as "of God." This might suggest God's claim over the town, even though the Philistines occupied it. 

- *group*: Prophets often lived in groups (for example, {{2 Kings 2:3|2 Kings 2:3}})

- *harps … lyres*: Ancient prophets sometimes used musical instruments to inspire and support their prophesying (for example, {{2 Kings 3:15|2 Kings 3:15}}).

- prophesy: See {{2 Samuel 23:2|2 Samuel 23:2}} and {{Acts 2:29-31|Acts 2:29–31}}.

- *different person*: Saul would become a spiritual and charismatic national leader (see {{1 Samuel 16:14|1 Samuel 16:14}}).
*God is with you*: This refers to God giving Saul the strength to do his duties.

- *Gilgal*: See the study note on 1 Samuel 7:16. 

- *Wait seven days*: Saul seems to have followed this instruction in {{1 Samuel 11:14-15|1 Samuel 11:14–15}} (compare with {{1 Samuel 13:8|13:8}}).
*God changed Saul’s heart*: God gave Saul courage and strength, helping him overcome his doubts and become king ({{1 Samuel 10:6|1 Samuel 10:6}}).

- *the Spirit of God rushed upon him*: See “The Spirit’s Presence” Theme Note; also see {{1 Samuel 11:6|1 Samuel 11:6}}; {{Judges 14:6|Judges 14:6}}, {{Judges 14:19|19}}; {{Judges 15:14|15:14}}; compare {{Acts 2:17-18|Acts 2:17–18}}, {{Acts 2:39|39}}).

- When Saul began to prophesy, it clearly showed he was chosen to lead Israel (see also {{1 Samuel 19:18-23|1 Samuel 19:18–23}}).

People who knew Saul might have thought he was not religious, making him an unlikely choice for a prophet. They might have been surprised and disappointed to get a prophet instead of a king (see {{John 6:14-15|John 6:14–15}}).

*“And who is their father?” So the saying became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”* Unlike priests and kings, prophets did not inherit their role. People might wonder why Saul, with a wealthy, famous father, would join a group with no notable background.
Saul might not have told his uncle because he was still unsure about what happened.

An earlier generation had gathered at Mizpah to nearly destroy the tribe of Benjamin ({{Judges 20:1-4|Judges 20:1–4}}). This made Mizpah an ironic place to begin the reign of a king from the tribe of Benjamin.
*rescued you from … all the kingdoms*: Israel did not need a human king to save them. They needed God, but they rejected him ({{1 Samuel 10:19|1 Samuel 10:19}}).

- *rejected your God*: See also {{1 Samuel 8:7|1 Samuel 8:7}}. Israel did not trust God to protect and save them.

- Clans are smaller groups within tribes.

- *rights of kingship*: See {{Deuteronomy 17:14-20|Deuteronomy 17:14–20}}. 

- *He wrote them*: Compare {{Exodus 24:4|Exodus 24:4}}; {{Joshua 24:26|Joshua 24:26}}.

- Samuel placed the document before the Lord, likely in the tabernacle. This act showed that God would reward those who followed the covenant and punish those who broke it.
*whose hearts God had touched*: God gave them confidence in Saul's ability to lead (see also {{1 Samuel 10:9|1 Samuel 10:9}}).
Saul showed he could lead by handling opposition and saving the town of Jabesh-gilead.

- These men were wicked (see {{1 Samuel 2:12|1 Samuel 2:12}}) because they disrespected God’s chosen king.

- People gave gifts to show respect ({{Genesis 32:13|Genesis 32:13}}, {{Genesis 32:18|18}}, {{Genesis 32:20|20}}), build political friendships ({{2 Kings 20:12|2 Kings 20:12}}), or show submission ({{Judges 3:15|Judges 3:15}}, {{Judges 3:17|17}}). 

- *Saul remained silent about it*: His calmness when insulted showed maturity. In contrast, {{Proverbs 16:14|Proverbs 16:14}} warns about a king’s anger when challenged. See also {{1 Samuel 11:12-13|1 Samuel 11:12–13}}.

- One Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript includes this additional paragraph that is not found in the Berean Standard Bible:

"Nahash, king of the Ammonites, had viciously oppressed the people of Gad and Reuben, gouging out the right eye of each Israelite dwelling there. He would not allow anyone to rescue them, and there was no Israelite east of the Jordan whose right eye had not been gouged out. But 7,000 men had escaped from the Ammonites and settled in Jabesh-gilead" (see the marginal note on {{1 Samuel 10:27|1 Samuel 10:27}} in the Berean Standard Bible).

Whether this material was part of the original text is uncertain. However, it helps explain the background of the conflict between Nahash and Jabesh-gilead and gives historical context for {{1 Samuel 11:1-15|1 Samuel 11:1–15}} (for example, {{1 Samuel 11:2|1 Samuel 11:2}}).

- Ammon (see {{Genesis 19:38|Genesis 19:38}}), located east of the Jordan River, was a threat to Israel like the Philistines in the southwest (see also {{Judges 10:6-11:33|Judges 10:6–11:33}}). 

- *Make a treaty with us*: Compare {{Joshua 9:1-27|Joshua 9}}; {{2 Samuel 10:19|2 Samuel 10:19}}.
Saul became king after winning a battle, which was why the people wanted a king ({{1 Samuel 8:20|1 Samuel 8:20}}).

*put out everyone’s right eye*: In the ancient Near East, it was common to mutilate captured soldiers. These soldiers, with one eye, lost depth perception, making it hard for them to fight in a revolt.
Nahash agreed to a seven-day delay, showing his arrogant confidence in winning and his desire to humiliate Israel as much as possible.
Not participating would indicate rejection of the leadership of both Saul as king and Samuel as prophet.

- Bezek was around 22.5 kilometers (14 miles) west of Jabesh-gilead. 

- The narrator's use of the terms Israel and Judah hints at the later division of the kingdom ({{1 Kings 12:1-33|1 Kings 12}}).
*No one shall be put to death*: This was a time to celebrate, not seek revenge.

*renew the kingship*: “Renew” indicates something was damaged or worn out and is now being restored (see {{Psalm 51:10|Psalm 51:10}}). The troublemakers ({{1 Samuel 10:27|1 Samuel 10:27}}; {{1 Samuel 11:12|11:12}}) may have shaken the people's confidence, but Saul's victory over the Ammonites fixed that.

- The formal ceremony before the Lord recognized Saul as king, while affirming that the Lord was Israel's true King.

- People often made peace offerings during important events that started significant institutions (see {{Exodus 24:5|Exodus 24:5}}; {{Leviticus 9:4|Leviticus 9:4}}, {{Leviticus 9:18|18}}, {{Leviticus 9:22|22}}; {{1 Kings 8:63-64|1 Kings 8:63–64}}).

The confirmation of Saul as king at Gilgal was the last step in making him king ({{1 Samuel 11:12-15|1 Samuel 11:12–15}}). It was also a suitable time for Samuel to give his farewell speech as Israel's leader.

- God chose Saul as the anointed one (see {{1 Samuel 9:16|1 Samuel 9:16}}). 

- *Whose ox or donkey have I taken?: *Compare with {{Numbers 16:15|Numbers 16:15}}. 

- *Whom have I cheated or oppressed?*: This contrasts with the actions of kings ({{1 Samuel 8:11-16|1 Samuel 8:11–16}}). 

- *have I accepted a bribe and closed my eyes?*: No, but Samuel’s sons did ({{1 Samuel 8:3|1 Samuel 8:3}}).

*you have not found anything in my hand*: Samuel's life and leadership in Israel were beyond criticism (see {{1 Corinthians 9:1-14|1 Corinthians 9:1–14}}; {{2 Corinthians 7:2|2 Corinthians 7:2}}; {{2 Corinthians 11:7-9|11:7–9}}; {{1 Thessalonians 2:1-12|1 Thessalonians 2:1–12}}). Saul, David, and Solomon, who were kings instead of prophetic judges, could not make this claim.
Moses and Aaron did not become leaders on their own. God appointed them as leaders.
In {{1 Samuel 12:1-5|1 Samuel 12:1–5}}, Samuel examined himself and was found innocent. In {{1 Samuel 12:6-25|1 Samuel 12:6–25}}, he examined the nation and found it guilty.

- *sold them into the hand*: See {{Judges 3:8|Judges 3:8}}; {{Judges 4:1-3|4:1–3}}. 

- *the king of Moab*: See {{Judges 3:12|Judges 3:12}}. Not all of Israel’s enemies during the time of the judges are listed (for example, the Ammonites and Midianites). This list highlights the significant events of that time.

- *Then they cried out to the LORD*: Sometimes suffering is what turns people’s hearts toward God. During the time of the judges, Israel often went through cycles of sin, oppression, repentance, and rescue. 

- *Baals and Ashtoreths*: When people turn away from God, they often turn to idols (see {{1 Samuel 7:3|1 Samuel 7:3}}; {{Judges 2:13|Judges 2:13}}; {{Judges 10:6|10:6}}). 

- Thinking that God must rescue us if we worship him turns worship into a cheap deal, where God must act to please someone. God deserves obedience and *worship* because he is God, not for the favors he can do.

- As in {{1 Samuel 12:9|1 Samuel 12:9}}, this list gives examples of some leaders.

- *Barak*: The Berean Standard Bible follows Greek and Syriac versions, which read "Barak" (see {{Judges 4:6-24|Judges 4:6–24}}; {{Judges 5:1|5:1}}, {{Judges 5:12|12}}, {{Judges 5:15|15}}). Some translations follow the Hebrew, which reads "Bedan." We are not sure who this judge is.

*when you saw that Nahash … was moving against you*: Israel's trouble with Nahash likely started before the events described in {{1 Samuel 11:1-11|1 Samuel 11:1–11}} (see {{1 Samuel 8:5|8:5}}, {{1 Samuel 8:20|20}}; {{1 Samuel 10:27|10:27}}).
Although the Israelites rejected God as their king, the Lord still granted their request (see study notes on 1 Samuel 8:7 and 8:8).
Worship means nothing if it does not lead to obedience.

To show that Israel still had to keep its covenant (promises between God and his people) even under a monarchy, Samuel used language from the Sinai covenant. This reminded the people that the Lord was always their true king (for example, {{Exodus 19:5-6|Exodus 19:5–6}}; {{Leviticus 26:1-46|Leviticus 26}}; {{Deuteronomy 30:11-20|Deuteronomy 30:11–20}}).
The wheat harvest happened in late spring or early summer when it rarely rained in Israel. Thunder and rain would show God's power as a sign of the people's wrongdoing in asking for a king.

- The people asked Samuel to pray for them (see also {{1 Samuel 7:8|1 Samuel 7:8}}) instead of praying themselves, likely because they were not close to God (notice they say "your God" instead of "our God"). 

- *added to all our sins*: Their sins included idol worship ({{1 Samuel 12:21|1 Samuel 12:21}}; see study note on 1 Samuel 8:8).
*worthless … they are empty*: Israel was slow to understand this lesson (for example, {{Isaiah 40:18-26|Isaiah 40:18–26}}; {{Isaiah 44:9-20|44:9–20}}).

- *for the sake of His great name*: He always keeps his promises, even if his people do not (see also {{Isaiah 37:35|Isaiah 37:35}}; {{Isaiah 43:25|43:25}}; {{Isaiah 48:9-11|48:9–11}}).

- *His people*: Israel, are his treasured possession (see {{Exodus 19:5|Exodus 19:5}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:25-29|Deuteronomy 9:25–29}}). He will never abandon them (see {{Romans 11:1-5|Romans 11:1–5}}, {{Romans 11:25-32|25–32}}).

- *I will continue to teach you*: Samuel was both a mediator and a teacher. 

- Although this speech ended Samuel's political leadership, he continued his spiritual work for a while (for example, {{1 Samuel 19:24|1 Samuel 19:24}}).

*swept away*: David later used this same Hebrew word for Saul’s death ({{1 Samuel 26:10|1 Samuel 26:10}}, “die … into battle”) and for his own possible death at Saul’s hands ({{1 Samuel 27:1|27:1}}, “get me”). This warning would continue to apply throughout Israel’s history as a monarchy (when it was ruled by kings).

- For the kings of Israel and Judah, Scripture usually records their age when they became king and how long they ruled (for example, {{2 Samuel 5:4-5|2 Samuel 5:4–5}}; {{1 Kings 14:21|1 Kings 14:21}}). 

- *thirty years old*: This age is likely when Saul became king. The Hebrew text and most Greek manuscripts leave out the number, making the original wording unclear.

- *reigned over Israel forty-two years*: See the textual note in the Berean Standard Bible. The Masoretic Text reads "over Israel two years." Most scholars think something is missing from the original manuscript, probably due to a copying mistake. Most English translations use *forty-two* based on the approximate number in {{Acts 13:21|Acts 13:21}}.

As Israel’s king, Saul made foolish decisions. He disobeyed God’s instructions about sacrificing animals at Gilgal. He did this because he was afraid. He thought he needed a large army to have victory in war.

He made his soldiers promise to go without food on the day of battle. He thought that fasting would give them favour with God in the battle. Yet none of those things mattered for their victory. Nor did it matter that the Israelites didn’t have weapons. God caused the Philistines to panic. This allowed the Israelites to have victory.

After that Saul was committed to carrying out his foolish promise to kill Jonathan. This was like Jephthah’s foolish promise after winning a battle (Judges 11:30­–40). But Saul’s soldiers had wisdom and were brave. They kept Saul from putting Jonathan to death.

Later, Saul didn’t fully obey God’s command about the Amalekites. They were to be set apart for God and completely destroyed. This was how God would bring judgement against the Amalekites. Instead, Saul kept many of their animals and allowed the king to live. All of these things showed that Saul was a foolish and proud king. He didn’t obey God’s commands about how kings should rule. He didn’t help the people to be faithful to God.

God was very sad about this and Samuel was very sad and angry. Samuel made it clear that Saul wouldn’t continue to be king over God’s people. This didn’t mean that Saul stopped ruling right away. It meant that the sons that came after Saul wouldn’t be kings. Someone from another family line would become king instead.

Saul lost power through three key events, similar to how he gained it (see study note on 1 Samuel 9:1–11:15):

- He offered the sacrifices himself instead of waiting for Samuel ({{1 Samuel 13:1-14|1 Samuel 13:1–14}}); 

- he made a hasty oath that endangered Jonathan's life ({{1 Samuel 14:1-46|1 Samuel 14:1–46}}); and

- he disobeyed God by not destroying the Amalekites and their possessions ({{1 Samuel 15:1-35|1 Samuel 15:1–35}}).

- Earlier, Saul had used 330,000 troops to fight a weaker enemy ({{1 Samuel 11:8|1 Samuel 11:8}}). Choosing 3,000 special troops here likely does not show overconfidence (compare {{Joshua 7:3-4|Joshua 7:3–4}}). Instead, Saul probably saw the need for a smaller, highly trained elite force to handle the troublesome Philistines (see {{1 Samuel 14:52|1 Samuel 14:52}}).

- Michmash was in Benjamin, about 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) northwest of Saul’s home in Gibeah.

- Geba was situated between Jonathan’s forces at Gibeah and Saul’s forces at Michmash. A deep gorge (a steep, narrow valley) separated Geba and Michmash (see {{1 Samuel 13:23|1 Samuel 13:23}}; {{1 Samuel 14:5|14:5}}). 

- The ram’s horn (*shofar* in Hebrew) was used to send signals, such as gathering an army ({{Judges 3:27|Judges 3:27}}). For other uses, see {{Leviticus 25:9|Leviticus 25:9}}; {{2 Samuel 6:15|2 Samuel 6:15}}; {{2 Samuel 15:10|15:10}}; {{2 Samuel 18:16|18:16}}; {{2 Samuel 20:1|20:1}}; {{Hosea 5:8|Hosea 5:8}}; {{Joel 2:15|Joel 2:15}}.

- Non-Israelites often used the term *Hebrews* in a disrespectful way (see {{1 Samuel 14:11|1 Samuel 14:11}}; {{1 Samuel 29:3|29:3}}; see also {{Genesis 39:14|Genesis 39:14}}; {{Genesis 43:32|43:32}}). Saul might have used it to bring pride to their identity.

- *Saul has attacked*: The leader often received credit for his soldiers' achievements.

- Saul's kingship was confirmed at Gilgal ({{1 Samuel 11:15|1 Samuel 11:15}}). Now, because of his disobedience, the Lord would reject his kingship there ({{1 Samuel 13:7-14|1 Samuel 13:7–14}}).

- The Israelites were greatly outnumbered, which made them afraid. 

- The Philistine army had 3,000 chariots and 6,000 charioteers, showing Israel's weaker position. In 1 Samuel, it never mentions Israel having any chariots (see study note on 1 Samuel 13:19–22).
The land of Gad and Gilead stretched along Transjordan, which is the area just east of the Jordan River.

*seven days for the time appointed by Samuel*: This was probably a different instruction from the one in {{1 Samuel 10:8|1 Samuel 10:8}}. It was likely given on another occasion (see study note on 1 Samuel 10:8).

*the burnt offering and the peace offerings*: These offerings (see {{Exodus 24:5|Exodus 24:5}}; {{Exodus 32:6|32:6}}; {{Numbers 10:10|Numbers 10:10}}; {{Numbers 15:8|15:8}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:6-7|Deuteronomy 27:6–7}}) were given during important events, whether dangerous or joyful. Usually, only priests made these sacrifices (but see study note on 1 Samuel 13:13).
*went out to greet him*: Saul did not seem to know he had done anything wrong.
*What have you done?*: Samuel’s question was a rebuke, not a request for information (compare {{Genesis 3:13|Genesis 3:13}}).

*sought the favor of the LORD*: The burnt offering aimed to ask God for victory in battle. Samuel had offered a similar sacrifice, which led to victory (see {{1 Samuel 7:7-11|1 Samuel 7:7–11}}). But Samuel, unlike Saul, served in a priestly role.

*the command that the LORD your God gave you*: Other kings offered sacrifices without criticism: 

- David ({{2 Samuel 6:13|2 Samuel 6:13}}, {{2 Samuel 6:17-18|17–18}}) 

- Solomon ({{1 Kings 3:15|1 Kings 3:15}}; {{1 Kings 8:64|8:64}}) 

- Ahaz {{2 Kings 16:12-13|2 Kings 16:12–13}}) 

Judges like Gideon ({{Judges 6:26|Judges 6:26}}) did the same. This shows that sometimes non-priests could perform sacrifices that pleased the Lord. However, Samuel, God's prophet, had instructed Saul to wait (see study note on 1 Samuel 13:8).
*A man after His own heart*: This prophecy refers to David (see also {{Acts 13:22|Acts 13:22}}) and not to Saul's son Jonathan. Rejecting Saul also meant rejecting his family's rule.
*about six hundred men* Most of the 3,000 troops ({{1 Samuel 13:2|1 Samuel 13:2}}) had left Saul ({{1 Samuel 13:6-7|1 Samuel 13:6–7}}).

Armies sent raiding groups to loot and spread fear among their enemies. These raiders went north to Ophrah, west to Beth-horon, and east to Zeboim. They avoided the south because the Israelites were strong there, and the terrain made it hard for forces to move easily (see study note on 1 Samuel 13:23).

*no blacksmith*: The Philistines prevented the Israelites from having weapons by controlling all the iron needed to make them. Iron technology was new in Canaan. It likely developed in the Aegean region and was brought to Canaan by seafaring people, like the Philistines.
The pass at Michmash was a key route through the canyon, separating Michmash from Geba, Gibeah, and other towns to the south.

- *bearing his armor*: See study note on 1 Samuel 16:21. 

- Jonathan did not tell his father because he knew Saul would not approve the dangerous plan. He also knew that Saul did not want anyone, not even his own son, to take honor away from him.
Jonathan again fought in his father's battles (see also {{1 Samuel 13:2-4|1 Samuel 13:2–4}}; {{1 Samuel 31:1-13|31}}).

Saul's actions in this chapter further support his removal as king ({{1 Samuel 13:8-14|1 Samuel 13:8–14}}; see also {{1 Samuel 15:1-35|15}}). Saul was estranged from both Samuel and his brave son Jonathan. {{1 Samuel 14:1-52|1 Samuel 14}} foreshadows Jonathan's important role in the shift from Saul's rule to David's.
*staying under*: Saul does nothing while Jonathan takes action (see also {{1 Samuel 22:6|1 Samuel 22:6}}).

- Ahijah the priest served as an adviser to Saul. He could seek God’s guidance for Saul by using the ephod (a sacred garment used to ask God for direction, {{1 Samuel 14:18-19|1 Samuel 14:18–19}}; see also {{1 Samuel 2:18|1 Samuel 2:18}} and study note on 1 Samuel 2:18; {{1 Samuel 23:9-10|1 Samuel 23:9–10}}).

- *son of Eli*: Saul, the rejected king ({{1 Samuel 13:13-14|1 Samuel 13:13–14}}), kept a priest from the rejected priesthood with him ({{1 Samuel 2:27-36|1 Samuel 2:27–36}}). 

- *Ichabod*: See {{1 Samuel 4:21|1 Samuel 4:21}}.
The Philistines controlled this area ({{1 Samuel 13:23|1 Samuel 13:23}}), so Jonathan and his armor bearer had to be careful.

- *uncircumcised men*: A word used to show strong dislike or disrespect for Israel’s enemies (see also {{1 Samuel 17:36|1 Samuel 17:36}}; {{1 Samuel 31:4|31:4}}). 

- *Perhaps*: Jonathan had no promise of survival, but he believed God could give them victory against the odds. Victory depended on God; Jonathan offered himself as a tool for God to use. 

- *whether by many or by few*: Jonathan understood what Gideon had learned long ago (see {{Judges 7:2-8|Judges 7:2–8}}).

- *Hebrews*: Refer to study note on 1 Samuel 13:3. 

- *out of the holes in which they were hiding*: See {{1 Samuel 13:6|1 Samuel 13:6}}.

- *terror struck*: This story is similar to Gideon's, showing Jonathan as a judge-like figure (see {{Judges 7:19-22|Judges 7:19–22}}). God had not officially chosen or specially empowered Jonathan as a leader, but God used him to save his people.

- *raiding parties*: See the study note on 1 Samuel 13:17–18.

*Bring … Israelites*: The Greek text of the Septuagint instead reads "Bring the ephod." The ark stayed at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years ({{1 Samuel 7:2|1 Samuel 7:2}}). Unlike the ephod, it was never used to predict the future (see study note on 1 Samuel 2:18).

Earlier, many Israelites hid because they were afraid ({{1 Samuel 13:6-7|1 Samuel 13:6–7}}). Some might have joined the Philistine army. The idea that they revolted when they had the chance suggests they might have been prisoners of war, forced to serve the Philistines.

- God saved Israel, not Saul. Jonathan acted willingly as the Lord worked through him.

- Beth-aven was directly west of Michmash (see {{1 Samuel 13:5|1 Samuel 13:5}}). The Israelites made the Philistines retreat all the way to Aijalon that day (see {{1 Samuel 14:31|1 Samuel 14:31}}).

- By making them swear an oath, Saul forced his tired, hungry men to abstain from food. This oath likely aimed to manipulate God for a good outcome, like the pagans might do (see notes on Exodus 23:26; 25:22; 32:4). 

- Saul's use of *my enemies* instead of "our enemies" shows his self-centered pride.

*brought trouble*: Joshua used this word when speaking to Achan ({{Joshua 7:25|Joshua 7:25}}), and Jephthah used it with his innocent daughter ({{Judges 11:35|Judges 11:35}}). Saul's foolish promise limited Israel's victory ({{1 Samuel 14:30|1 Samuel 14:30}}) and endangered his son's life (see also {{Joshua 6:18|Joshua 6:18}}; {{1 Chronicles 2:7|1 Chronicles 2:7}}).
*Aijalon*: If the Philistines ran away through Beth-horon, the Israelites chased them for about 32 kilometers (nearly 20 miles).

The men were very hungry, so they ate meat without draining the blood. This act broke God's law (see {{Leviticus 17:10-14|Leviticus 17:10–14}}) and was a sin against the Lord. To stop more sin, Saul used a large rock as a field altar to properly drain the animals' blood. This incident happened because of Saul's foolish oath.
*the first time he had built an altar*: This is the only altar mentioned. David later built another altar, which became the site of God's temple ({{2 Samuel 24:18-25|2 Samuel 24:18–25}}).
*God did not answer*: Neither the "no" nor the "yes" answer from the Urim and Thummim appeared.

Priests cast sacred lots by using the Urim and Thummim to learn what God wanted them to do ({{Exodus 28:30|Exodus 28:30}}; {{Leviticus 8:8|Leviticus 8:8}}). David also used them to seek God's guidance ({{1 Samuel 23:2|1 Samuel 23:2}}; {{1 Samuel 30:8|30:8}}; {{2 Samuel 2:1|2 Samuel 2:1}}). The Urim and Thummim were two small objects, possibly flat stones, sticks, or arrows, used like dice. They would give a positive, neutral, or negative answer.
The people, aware of God’s blessing on the real hero of the day, were wiser than their king.

- *assumed *(literally *took*): Samuel often used this verb to describe a king's actions: “*He will take … take … take*” ({{1 Samuel 8:10-18|1 Samuel 8:10–18}}).

- *the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Edomites … Zobah*: David faced these enemies during his reign and expanded Israel’s territory (see {{2 Samuel 8:1-14|2 Samuel 8:1–14}}).

Unlike the foolishness mentioned in {{1 Samuel 14:1-46|1 Samuel 14:1–46}}, these verses highlight Saul's military victories. Each king's reign in 1 Samuel—2 Kings ends with a similar summary of achievements.

*defeated the Amalekites*: See {{1 Samuel 15:1-35|1 Samuel 15:1–35}}. The Amalekites were a nomadic group (people who move from place to place rather than living in one town) in the south. They often attacked Israel by raiding villages and taking goods (see {{Exodus 17:8-16|Exodus 17:8–16}}; {{Numbers 14:45|Numbers 14:45}}; {{Judges 3:13|Judges 3:13}}; {{Judges 6:3|6:3}}, {{Judges 6:33|33}}; {{Judges 7:12|7:12}}; {{Judges 10:12|10:12}}).

- *sons of Saul were*: Saul had another son named Abinadab ({{1 Samuel 31:2|1 Samuel 31:2}}).

- *Ishvi*: This is another name for Ish-bosheth (which means “man of shame”). He was also called Esh-baal (“man of Baal”). He briefly ruled as a rival king over the northern tribes during David’s early years ({{2 Samuel 2:8-11|2 Samuel 2:8–11}}).
This information about Saul’s family, placed here instead of at the end of his reign, suggests his reign was nearly over and none of his sons would succeed him.

Ahinoam is only mentioned in Saul's story here. In {{1 Samuel 25:43|1 Samuel 25:43}}, David marries a woman named Ahinoam. These might be the same person, but it is unclear (see {{2 Samuel 12:8|2 Samuel 12:8}}).

- Saul easily defeated the Ammonites ({{1 Samuel 11:11|1 Samuel 11:11}}), but he struggled against the Philistines. The Philistines had a strong army and controlled iron and bronze ({{1 Samuel 13:19-22|1 Samuel 13:19–22}}). 

- *Saul would enlist him*: Samuel had warned earlier that the king would take people and possessions ({{1 Samuel 8:11|1 Samuel 8:11}}).
After Saul disobeyed God by not completely destroying the Amalekites, God rejected him more strongly than before (see {{1 Samuel 13:8-14|1 Samuel 13:8–14}}).

*LORD of Hosts*: See study note on 1 Samuel 1:3. 

*I witnessed*: In the time of Moses, the nation of Amalek lived in southern Judah and the Negev area south of Judah. As Israel traveled to Canaan, the Amalekites attacked the sick, weak, and those at the back of the group. They were the first to attack Israel after the exodus from Egypt, for which God had promised to judge them ({{Exodus 17:8-16|Exodus 17:8–16}}; {{Deuteronomy 25:17-19|Deuteronomy 25:17–19}}).
*devote to destruction*: See "Complete Dedication" Theme Note.
*Telaim*: This might be the same as Telem (see {{Joshua 15:24|Joshua 15:24}}).
The unnamed town in the valley was near a Negev *wadi* (a dry streambed that fills with water only when it rains).

- The Kenites were wandering metalworkers and descendants of the father-in-law of Moses ({{Judges 1:16|Judges 1:16}}). 

- *You showed kindness*: See {{Exodus 18:1-27|Exodus 18}}; {{Numbers 10:29-32|Numbers 10:29–32}}.
The area where the Amalekites lived stretched from Havilah in northern Sinai to Shur near the eastern border of Egypt.
Agag was likely a descendant of an earlier king with the same name (see {{Numbers 24:7|Numbers 24:7}}; compare {{Esther 3:1|Esther 3:1}}).

Saul and his men ignored the Lord's order to devote the Amalekites to destruction ({{1 Samuel 15:3|1 Samuel 15:3}}). Even though the whole army disobeyed God's command, Saul was responsible as their leader.

- Carmel was a town near Hebron in southern Judah. 

- Saul celebrated his achievements by building a monument to himself, but he actually deserved shame ({{1 Samuel 15:16-19|1 Samuel 15:16–19}}). 

- *Gilgal*: See {{1 Samuel 13:4|1 Samuel 13:4}}.

*I have carried out the LORD’s instructions*: Compare with {{1 Samuel 15:3|1 Samuel 15:3}}. Saul believed his actions were justified ({{1 Samuel 15:15|1 Samuel 15:15}}; compare with {{Leviticus 22:19|Leviticus 22:19}}). However, Samuel exposed Saul’s false excuse ({{1 Samuel 15:17-19|1 Samuel 15:17–19}}). Samuel then carried out God’s command himself ({{1 Samuel 15:32-33|1 Samuel 15:32–33}}).
Saul blamed the army even though he was the commander. His true motivation was not spiritual ({{1 Samuel 15:9|1 Samuel 15:9}}).
As the anointed king of Israel, Saul was responsible for disobeying God. False humility or excuses could not lessen this responsibility.

- *The troops*: Saul kept blaming others (see {{1 Samuel 15:15|1 Samuel 15:15}}). 

- Gilgal was a religious center. Saul tried to use religion to excuse disobeying God.

- *Does the LORD delight*: God values obedience more than ritual acts (see also {{Psalm 40:6|Psalm 40:6}}; {{Hosea 6:6|Hosea 6:6}}; {{Matthew 12:7|Matthew 12:7}}). 

- *the fat of rams*: People offered the best parts of the animal to God.

- *Rebellion … and arrogance*: These sins of the heart are as bad as the sinful practices of idol-worshipping pagans.

- Scripture condemns witchcraft (see study note on Deuteronomy 18:10).

- *I feared the people*: Saul kept blaming others (see {{1 Samuel 15:15|1 Samuel 15:15}}, {{1 Samuel 15:21|21}}).

- *obeyed their voice*: The chapter does not suggest any pressure from them. Saul’s confession seems dishonest (compare with David, {{2 Samuel 12:13|2 Samuel 12:13}}; {{Psalm 51:1-19|Psalm 51}}).
Saul admitted his wrongdoing, but it was too late and he still made excuses.
Saul soon found out who the other person was ({{1 Samuel 18:8-9|1 Samuel 18:8–9}}; compare with chapter {{1 Samuel 16:1-23|16}}).

*does not lie or change His mind*: Samuel spoke about God's promise to make David king and protect his family line. God had rejected Saul, but he would never reject David (see {{2 Samuel 7:8-17|2 Samuel 7:8–17}}).
*honor me now before the elders*: To help Saul maintain his dignity.

- The verb phrase *mourned* usually means grieving over someone's death. Although Saul was still alive, his rule as king was ending. Samuel might have been grieving due to personal attachment to Saul, feeling like he failed, or worrying that Israel's situation would worsen. 

- *the LORD regretted*: See “God’s Change of Mind” Theme Note.

- *How long are you going to mourn*: See study note on 1 Samuel 15:35. 

- Bethlehem is about five miles south of Jerusalem. It later became known as the City of David ({{Luke 2:11|Luke 2:11}}) and is the birthplace of Jesus. 

- Jesse was the grandson of Boaz and Ruth ({{Ruth 4:22|Ruth 4:22}}). 

- *I have selected*: This Hebrew verb means God saw one of Jesse's sons and chose him based on what he saw. God, the eternal king, knows better than the people of Israel how to choose a good king to serve the nation. He provided a replacement for Saul who would lead Israel well.

David replaced Saul as king. David and Saul were alike in these ways: 

- Samuel anointed both.

- Neither was pursuing the position of king.

- Both were unlikely choices (Saul was from the smallest tribe, and David was the youngest son).

- They were both good-looking ({{1 Samuel 9:2|1 Samuel 9:2}}; {{1 Samuel 16:12|16:12}}).

- The Spirit *rushed upon* each when anointed as king ({{1 Samuel 10:10|1 Samuel 10:10}}; {{1 Samuel 11:6|11:6}}; {{1 Samuel 16:13|16:13}}).

The main difference was that David was "a man after [God's] own heart" ({{1 Samuel 13:14|1 Samuel 13:14}}; compare {{1 Samuel 16:7|16:7}}), while Saul was not.

God chose a shepherd named David to be the next king of Israel.

Saul didn’t know that Samuel had anointed David and that God’s Spirit was with David. Saul took David from his father Jesse to be his servant. Samuel had warned the Israelites that a king would do that. David served Saul by carrying his armour and playing the harp for him. The music helped Saul calm down when he was troubled and feeling terrified.

Saul had changed from when he first became king. He had started as a humble farmer who was willing to be used by God’s Spirit. He became a mighty fighter as king. But then he became proud and foolish. He was no longer willing to be used by God. And so God’s Spirit left him. After that Saul became even more fearful. He was so terrified that he wouldn’t fight Goliath.

Goliath was a huge and strong Philistine soldier. Only David was willing to fight him. David was a brave and clever fighter. He had complete trust in God to save him. Goliath used the names of his false gods to curse David. David fought against Goliath in the name of the Lord. God gave David victory. This showed that God was more powerful than the false gods of the Philistines.

*say, ‘I have come to sacrifice'*: God sometimes guides his followers into risky situations. He protects them, sometimes through miracles, sometimes through strategy (compare {{Exodus 3:18-22|Exodus 3:18–22}}). As a priestly judge, Samuel would not have seemed suspicious by offering a sacrifice (see {{1 Samuel 10:8|1 Samuel 10:8}}).
*The elders … trembled*: The elders were afraid because news had likely reached Bethlehem that Samuel had rebuked Saul and put Agag to death.

- *Consecrate yourselves*: Self-purification involved bathing and avoiding sexual activity (see {{Exodus 19:10-15|Exodus 19:10–15}}; compare {{Genesis 35:2-4|Genesis 35:2–4}}).

- The sacrifice probably happened the next morning (see {{Numbers 11:18|Numbers 11:18}}; {{Joshua 3:5|Joshua 3:5}}; {{Joshua 7:13-14|7:13–14}}).

- Samuel conducted the purification ritual for Jesse and his sons to prepare them for the sacrifice and the anointing of the new king (compare {{Exodus 19:10|Exodus 19:10}}; {{Joshua 3:5|Joshua 3:5}}).

- *his appearance or height*: Like Saul, Eliab, Jesse’s oldest son, looked impressive (see {{1 Samuel 9:2|1 Samuel 9:2}}). But like Saul, God rejected him (see {{1 Samuel 15:23|1 Samuel 15:23}}). God had chosen someone else to anoint as king. 

- *the LORD sees the heart*: God can give a new heart (see {{1 Samuel 10:9|1 Samuel 10:9}}), touch hearts (see {{1 Samuel 10:26|10:26}}), and understand deep motivations (see {{Psalm 139:1|Psalm 139:1}}). God sees what people cannot. God sees a person’s true character. Eliab’s character is revealed in {{1 Samuel 17:28|1 Samuel 17:28}}.

- The *Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David*, and this was clear in many instances (for example, {{1 Samuel 16:23|1 Samuel 16:23}}; {{1 Samuel 17:48-54|17:48–54}}; {{1 Samuel 18:5|18:5}}, {{1 Samuel 18:12-16|12–16}}). The Spirit of the Lord had also come upon Saul ({{1 Samuel 10:10|1 Samuel 10:10}}) but left him due to his disobedience ({{1 Samuel 16:14|1 Samuel 16:14}}).

- Ramah is Samuel’s hometown ({{1 Samuel 1:1|1 Samuel 1:1}}).

- *the Spirit of the LORD had departed from Saul*: This contrasts with David, who received the Spirit (see “The Spirit’s Presence” Theme Note).

- The Lord sent a tormenting spirit because of Saul's disobedience (see also {{1 Samuel 18:10|1 Samuel 18:10}}; {{1 Samuel 19:9|19:9}}; compare {{Judges 9:23|Judges 9:23}}; {{Romans 1:28-29|Romans 1:28–29}}).
After God’s Spirit left Saul, his rule continued to fail. His time as king ended in shame and military defeat ({{1 Samuel 31:1-13|1 Samuel 31}}).

- *harp*: The instrument was likely a lyre, a small stringed instrument used for music (as in {{1 Samuel 10:5|1 Samuel 10:5}}).

- *the LORD is with him*: People saw that God's Spirit was with David ({{1 Samuel 16:13|1 Samuel 16:13}}).

- At first, Saul loved David very much, but this love soon became intense jealousy and hatred (see {{1 Samuel 18:8-14|1 Samuel 18:8–14}}). 

- An armor bearer in ancient Israel was the personal assistant of a warrior leader (see {{1 Samuel 14:1-15|1 Samuel 14:1–15}}; {{1 Samuel 31:4-6|31:4–6}}; {{Judges 9:54|Judges 9:54}}; {{2 Samuel 18:15|2 Samuel 18:15}}).
David's father, Jesse ({{1 Samuel 16:18|1 Samuel 16:18}}), made sure David could serve Saul and still take care of his sheep at home (see {{1 Samuel 17:14-15|1 Samuel 17:14–15}}).

- *Saul would become well*: David was not just a handsome young man with musical talent. He was the chosen king. David showed what a king should be: someone who brings relief. Later, David wrote many psalms that have provided comfort and relief over the years.

- *the spirit of distress would depart from him*: Even those who are disobedient and rejected can find relief and comfort through the Lord’s servant.

- The Philistines were a constant threat during Saul’s rule (see {{1 Samuel 14:47-52|1 Samuel 14:47–52}}).

- Socoh in Judah was 22.5 kilometers (14 miles) west of Bethlehem, near Philistine land.

- Azekah was a few kilometers northwest of Socoh (the exact location of Ephes-dammim is unknown). The Philistines were invading Israelite territory.
The Valley of Elah was a fertile area running east to west, located 24 kilometers (15 miles) southwest of Bethlehem.

- *champion*: In ancient times, opposing forces would sometimes let chosen individuals from each side settle a conflict. This reduced casualties and other costs. This type of combat is shown in {{2 Samuel 2:12-17|2 Samuel 2:12–17}}. 

- Gath was one of five Philistine cities known for having giants as citizens ({{2 Samuel 21:15-22|2 Samuel 21:15–22}}).
Goliath was a huge, fully armored warrior, but he did not have God (a much stronger ally) on his side ({{1 Samuel 17:45-47|1 Samuel 17:45–47}}).
*Ephrathite*: This means a person from Ephrath, which is another name for Bethlehem ({{Genesis 35:19|Genesis 35:19}}; {{1 Chronicles 4:4|1 Chronicles 4:4}}).

*went back and forth*: He worked as a musician and armor bearer for Saul (see {{1 Samuel 16:19-23|1 Samuel 16:19–23}}) while also managing his responsibilities at home. This irregular service might explain why Saul did not recognize David during the encounter with Goliath (see {{1 Samuel 17:55-58|1 Samuel 17:55–58}}).

- *What will be done for the man*: Compare with {{1 Samuel 18:17-27|1 Samuel 18:17–27}}. David wanted a reward, but he was more focused on stopping Goliath from insulting God ({{1 Samuel 17:45-47|1 Samuel 17:45–47}}). 

- *uncircumcised*: See study note on 1 Samuel 14:6.
Eliab was angry, possibly because he was jealous that David was chosen to be king instead of him ({{1 Samuel 16:6-13|1 Samuel 16:6–13}}).
*Your servant will go and fight him*: David showed courage, while Saul showed fear ({{1 Samuel 17:11|1 Samuel 17:11}}).

- A stream flowed through the valley of Elah ({{1 Samuel 17:2|1 Samuel 17:2}}). 

- A sling was a leather pouch with two leather straps. When spun quickly with a stone inside, releasing one strap would launch the stone at a target. David likely became very skilled with a sling as a shepherd, but warriors also used slings ({{Judges 20:16|Judges 20:16}}).

- *ruddy*: The same Hebrew word is translated “red” ({{Genesis 25:25|Genesis 25:25}}). Here, it highlights David’s youth and inexperience.

- *boy*: Saul had expressed similar disbelief ({{1 Samuel 17:33|1 Samuel 17:33}}). Goliath, as a champion, expected to face an Israelite warrior of equal status.

- *a dog*: This phrase is a metaphor (a word picture) for a low-status servant who bows and obeys others. Goliath used it to insult David and treat him as worthless (see {{2 Samuel 9:8|2 Samuel 9:8}}). 

- *sticks*: David had hidden his sling. Goliath could see only David’s staff, so he thought David was coming with a simple weapon.

- *by his gods*: Goliath called on his gods, so David's win would also show God's victory over Dagon, the main god of the Philistines (see {{1 Samuel 5:2|1 Samuel 5:2}}, {{1 Samuel 5:5|5}}).
A body left for scavengers like birds and wild animals was considered severely cursed (see {{Deuteronomy 21:23|Deuteronomy 21:23}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:26|28:26}}).
*the LORD of Hosts*: See study note on 1 Samuel 1:3. Even though the Philistines seemed stronger, David understood that Israel had the ultimate advantage with the one true God.

- Goliath's forehead was exposed under his very large helmet.

- *he fell facedown*: The stone only knocked Goliath out; David killed him by cutting off his head ({{1 Samuel 17:51|1 Samuel 17:51}}).

- The Israelites chased the Philistines to Gath, which is about 9.7 kilometers (6 miles) west. 

- Ekron, a Philistine city, is 8 kilometers (5 miles) north of Gath. 

- Shaaraim, a city in Judah, is near Azekah ({{1 Samuel 17:1|1 Samuel 17:1}}).
