Unless specifically forbidden (for example, {{1 Samuel 15:3|1 Samuel 15:3}}; {{Joshua 6:18|Joshua 6:18}}), winning a battle allowed taking war spoils ({{Deuteronomy 2:35|Deuteronomy 2:35}}; {{Joshua 8:2|Joshua 8:2}}).

Jerusalem became an Israelite city when David captured it from the Jebusites ({{2 Samuel 5:6-7|2 Samuel 5:6–7}}). Jerusalem was likely where David took Goliath's head after he became king. However, David might have brought it to Jerusalem earlier to scare the non-Israelite residents.

Considering {{1 Samuel 16:14-23|1 Samuel 16:14–23}}, it is surprising that neither Saul nor Abner recognized David. The events in {{1 Samuel 17:1-58|1 Samuel 17}} might have occurred either before or long after David's occasional service mentioned in {{1 Samuel 16:1-23|1 Samuel 16}}. Saul likely ruled as king for forty-two years, as noted in {{1 Samuel 13:1|1 Samuel 13:1}}.

- David and Jonathan shared many similarities, both were: 

- young and capable,

- military heroes,

- had strong faith in God, and

- had claims to Israel's throne (each had a reason he could become king).

Jonathan's true character showed when he recognized and supported God's choice of David as the next king of Israel (see {{1 Samuel 18:3-4|1 Samuel 18:3–4}}; {{1 Samuel 20:12-17|20:12–17}}). 

- *Jonathan loved him as himself*: See {{1 Samuel 20:17|1 Samuel 20:17}}; {{2 Samuel 1:26|2 Samuel 1:26}}. Others in this chapter are also said to love David: 

- all Israel and Judah ({{1 Samuel 18:16|1 Samuel 18:16}}),

- Saul’s daughter Michal ({{1 Samuel 18:20|1 Samuel 18:20}}), and

- Saul’s servants ({{1 Samuel 18:22|1 Samuel 18:22}}).

Some modern interpreters suggest a romantic relationship between David and Jonathan. However, the biblical text describes their relationship as a deep and loyal friendship.

Saul’s family members loved David. Jonathan made a covenant of friendship with David that would last for ever. Jonathan accepted that God chose David to be Israel’s next king. He wanted to support David when David was king. He protected David from Saul many times.

Saul’s daughter Michal was in love with David. As David’s wife, she was willing to lie to her father to protect David. David had more and more success as an officer in Saul’s army. But Saul was controlled more and more by fear and jealousy. He refused to accept that God had chosen David to be king.

Instead of turning back to God, Saul tried over and over to kill David. First he sent David into battles hoping that he would be killed while fighting. Then Saul tried to kill Jonathan for protecting David. After that, David ran away from Saul. Saul had an entire town of priests killed because Ahimelek helped David. This showed that Saul had no respect for people who were anointed to serve God.

Many soldiers and their families joined David when he ran away from Saul. So did Abiathar the priest. But many other Israelites were willing to hand David over to Saul. Even so, David and his men still rescued the Israelites from the Philistines.
David used to work for Saul part-time (see {{1 Samuel 17:15|1 Samuel 17:15}} and study note on 1 Samuel 17:15), but now Saul kept David with him all the time.

Because Jonathan loved David and knew God had chosen David to be Israel's next king (see {{1 Samuel 20:13-17|1 Samuel 20:13–17}}, {{1 Samuel 20:30-31|30–31}}; {{1 Samuel 23:17|23:17}}), he made a serious promise of friendship with him. Jonathan gave David items that showed his status as the king's son and crown prince, symbolically passing his right to be the next king to David.

*thousands … tens of thousands*: This very large increase in numbers between two lines of Hebrew poetry was a way of making the statement stronger (see {{Deuteronomy 32:30|Deuteronomy 32:30}}; {{Psalm 91:7|Psalm 91:7}}). Because of his great military victories, David was beginning to become more popular and more successful than Saul ({{1 Samuel 18:16|1 Samuel 18:16}}, {{1 Samuel 18:30|30}}; {{1 Samuel 21:11|21:11}}).
Saul came to view David as a threat rather than an ally and would do anything to get rid of him.
In his jealousy and fear, Saul would have been happier with one dead David than with thousands of dead Philistines ({{1 Samuel 18:7|18:7}}).
The Lord had departed from Saul as king as punishment for his disobedience. Saul’s kingship would fail, and David’s would succeed ({{1 Samuel 18:14|1 Samuel 18:14}}).

Saul promised his daughter to anyone who could kill Goliath ({{1 Samuel 17:25|1 Samuel 17:25}}; see also {{Joshua 15:16|Joshua 15:16}}; {{Judges 1:12|Judges 1:12}}). But he added more risks for David (see also {{1 Samuel 18:21|1 Samuel 18:21}}, {{1 Samuel 18:25|25}}).
Saul offered his older daughter, Merab, to David. But he did not truly intend to give Merab to David.

*Who am I, and what is my family*: This shows humility (see also {{2 Samuel 7:18|2 Samuel 7:18}}; compare {{Exodus 3:11|Exodus 3:11}}). David's family could not pay the bride price to marry the king's daughter ({{1 Samuel 18:23-25|1 Samuel 18:23–25}}).
*So*: Or *But.* Either David did not accept the offer, or Saul did not keep his promise.
*is pleased with you*: The same Hebrew word describes Jonathan’s love for David ({{1 Samuel 18:3|1 Samuel 18:3}}; {{1 Samuel 19:1-2|19:1–2}}). Here, it was completely untrue.
A future son-in-law would give a *bride price* (a required gift) to his bride’s father (see {{Genesis 34:12|Genesis 34:12}}; {{Exodus 22:16-17|Exodus 22:16–17}}).
*even more afraid*: Saul’s fear was not justified. Even when Saul treated David as an enemy, David continued to honor Saul as king (see {{1 Samuel 24:1-22|1 Samuel 24;}} {{1 Samuel 26:1-25|26}}).
Jonathan addressed his father as the king to show respect.

*swore an oath*: Breaking a vow is a serious offense against God (see {{Numbers 30:2|Numbers 30:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 23:21-23|Deuteronomy 23:21–23}}; compare {{Ecclesiastes 5:4-5|Ecclesiastes 5:4–5}}). However, Saul soon ignored his promise and tried to kill David again ({{1 Samuel 19:9-24|1 Samuel 19:9–24}}).
*tried to pin him to the wall with his spear*: See also {{1 Samuel 18:11|1 Samuel 18:11}}; {{1 Samuel 20:33|20:33}}.

- *A household idol*: The Hebrew word *teraphim* refers to household idols (small images used in homes, often for worship or protection). These idols appear in several Old Testament passages, such as {{Genesis 31:30|Genesis 31:30}}; {{Judges 17:5|Judges 17:5}}; and {{2 Kings 23:24|2 Kings 23:24}}. Having an idol in David and Michal's home might show how common pagan idol worship was among the Israelites. The idol might have belonged to Michal. David did not seem to object to Michal having it. (Compare to Rachel stealing her father’s household idols in {{Genesis 31:19|Genesis 31:19}}.) 

- Siblings Jonathan ({{1 Samuel 19:1-7|1 Samuel 19:1–7}}) and Michal ({{1 Samuel 19:11-18|19:11–18}}) saved David from their father and disrupted their father’s plans to harm him. Members of Saul’s royal family were important in David’s rise, though David did not take Saul’s throne by force.

- *Ramah*: This was Samuel’s hometown ({{1 Samuel 1:1|1 Samuel 1:1}}).

- Naioth was a small village near another Ramah in the region of Benjamin.

- Prophets often assembled in groups under a single leader (see {{2 Kings 2:15|2 Kings 2:15}}; {{2 Kings 4:38|4:38}}; {{2 Kings 6:1-7|6:1–7}}).

- The Spirit of God came upon Saul’s men to allow David to escape ({{1 Samuel 20:1|1 Samuel 20:1}}).
*messengers … a third time*: Each time Saul sent troops, the Spirit captured David's would-be captors. Prophesying distracted them from chasing David.

- When Saul tore off his clothes and lay naked (that is, without his royal garments), he unknowingly showed his true spiritual condition. God had stripped him of the kingship. Earlier passages explain this rejection ({{1 Samuel 13:14|1 Samuel 13:14}}; {{1 Samuel 15:10-11|15:10–11}}, {{1 Samuel 15:23|23}}; see “Prophetic Sign Acts” Theme Note).

- *Is Saul also among the prophets?*: In {{1 Samuel 10:9-13|1 Samuel 10:9–13}}, Saul was rising as God’s chosen king. Here, he is moving downward under the weight of God’s rejection.
Jonathan did not understand his father's plans. David's willingness to swear by the Lord showed he was sure about Saul's intentions.

*New Moon*: The ancient Hebrews used a lunar calendar, and the new moon signaled a new month. They started each month with a special sacrifice ({{Numbers 28:11-15|Numbers 28:11–15}}), which became a monthly festival.
Israelite families might choose a new moon festival for their yearly family sacrifice (see, for example, {{1 Samuel 1:3|1 Samuel 1:3}}).

- *kindness*: The Hebrew word *ḥesed* means faithful love or commitment. It describes faithfulness between people who are bound by a covenant (a binding agreement).

- *a covenant*: A covenant is a serious and binding agreement that includes promises and loyalty. David and Jonathan made such an agreement with each other (see {{1 Samuel 18:3|1 Samuel 18:3}}; {{1 Samuel 20:16|20:16}}).

- *may the LORD punish me*: Jonathan promised David he would keep his promise.

- *as He has been with my father*: Jonathan saw that God blessed David as God had once blessed his father. The divine favor that made Saul king ({{1 Samuel 9:14-10:1|1 Samuel 9:14–10:1}}) would now make David king as Saul's replacement. Jonathan accepted this, even though he was Saul's natural successor.

*loving devotion*: The Hebrew word *ḥesed* refers to loyal love and faithfulness to a covenant (see study note on 1 Samuel 20:8). Jonathan reminded David to keep his commitment to him when David became king. Jonathan’s concern was reasonable. In the ancient world, a new king might kill members of the former royal family to remove rivals to the throne. Saul later made a similar request of David ({{1 Samuel 24:21|1 Samuel 24:21}}).
*cut off your loving devotion from my household*: David later cared for Jonathan’s son, Mephibosheth, like his own son ({{2 Samuel 9:1-13|2 Samuel 9:1–13}}).

Jonathan's plan would allow David to get the message even if there could be no face-to-face meeting. The boy's presence reduced suspicion and gave Jonathan an excuse to go to the field. As it happened, only the boy went with Jonathan to the field. When the boy left, David could talk to Jonathan directly ({{1 Samuel 20:40-42|1 Samuel 20:40–42}}).
Abner was Saul’s cousin and served as commander of Saul’s army ({{1 Samuel 14:50|1 Samuel 14:50}}; {{1 Samuel 17:55|17:55}}). His importance is shown by his position beside the king at this festival.

- A number of circumstances could render a person ceremonially unclean and thus unfit for attending a sacred festival (see {{Leviticus 7:20-21|Leviticus 7:2–21}}). Often, an unclean person was required to be excluded from such functions only until the evening of the same day ({{Leviticus 15:1-33|Leviticus 15}}). This explains why Saul became suspicious after David did not arrive the next day. 

- Saul referred to David as the son of Jesse (also in {{1 Samuel 20:31|1 Samuel 20:31}}; {{1 Samuel 22:7|22:7}}), a description that functioned as David’s last name.
*let me go*: This verb also describes how David escaped from Saul earlier ({{1 Samuel 19:10-12|1 Samuel 19:10–12}}, {{1 Samuel 19:17-18|17–18}}).

- *You son of a perverse and rebellious woman!*: This insult was as strong and offensive in Hebrew as it is in English. 

- *to your own shame*: Saul cared about his family's legacy. He saw David’s actions as a threat to Jonathan, the rightful heir. To Saul, Jonathan was stupidly hurting and *shaming* himself by supporting David.

- *Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan*: Saul had tried to kill others in this same way before (see also {{1 Samuel 18:11|1 Samuel 18:11}}; {{1 Samuel 19:10|19:10}}). 

- *so Jonathan knew*: Jonathan had been slow to accept the truth about his own father ({{1 Samuel 20:2-3|1 Samuel 20:2–3}}). Now he could no longer deny it.

- *David … bowed*: Jonathan had a higher social rank, making David's gesture appropriate. 

- *he and Jonathan … wept*: For the first time in the story, the text shows that both men openly shared their grief (see {{1 Samuel 18:1|1 Samuel 18:1}}, {{1 Samuel 18:3-4|3–4}}; {{1 Samuel 20:17|20:17}}).
*sworn in the name of the LORD*: (See {{1 Samuel 18:3|1 Samuel 18:3}}; {{1 Samuel 20:15-17|20:15–17}}; {{1 Samuel 23:16-18|23:16–18}}).

- Nob was just north of Jerusalem, in southern Benjamin's territory. 

- Ahimelech the priest was a descendant of the condemned family of Eli ({{1 Samuel 14:3|1 Samuel 14:3}}; {{1 Samuel 22:9|22:9}}). 

- The elders of Bethlehem were afraid when Samuel suddenly came to their city to anoint David as Saul’s replacement ({{1 Samuel 16:4|1 Samuel 16:4}}). A similar fear appears here. In both situations, a well-known person who had problems with Saul arrived without warning. Both Ahimelech and the elders of Bethlehem feared that Saul might accuse them of helping an enemy of the king. Such suspicion could lead to death. In this case, what they feared did happen (see {{1 Samuel 22:9-19|1 Samuel 22:9–19}}).
*“The king has given me a mission,”*: David lied to hide that he was an outlaw and to ease Ahimelech's concerns.

- Only priests could eat the holy bread (see {{Exodus 25:22-30|Exodus 25:22–30}}; {{Leviticus 24:5-9|Leviticus 24:5–9}}), and only within sacred areas. 

- *kept themselves from women*: The holy bread was for those who were ceremonially pure. The priest checked that David’s men were not ceremonially impure from sexual activity (see {{Leviticus 15:16-18|Leviticus 15:16–18}}). Normally, people who were not priests could not eat this bread. The priest made an exception because he saw the men's needs and believed they were on a royal mission.

- *gave him the consecrated bread*: Jesus referred to this event to show that helping people is more important than strict obedience to religious rules (see {{Matthew 12:1-8|Matthew 12:1–8}}; {{Mark 2:23-28|Mark 2:23–28}}; {{Luke 6:1-5|Luke 6:1–5}}). 

- The Bread of the Presence included twelve loaves, possibly one for each tribe. The priests placed them on a table in the Holy Place. They were replaced every Sabbath (see {{Exodus 25:30|Exodus 25:30}}; {{Leviticus 24:5-9|Leviticus 24:5–9}}).

*detained before the LORD*: Ahimelech asked God for guidance on behalf of others ({{1 Samuel 22:15|1 Samuel 22:15}}). Because of this, Doeg may have been waiting for an answer to a question he had brought before God.

- David used Goliath's sword to cut off the giant's head ({{1 Samuel 17:51|1 Samuel 17:51}}). Both the sword and Goliath's head were taken as war trophies ({{1 Samuel 17:54|17:54}}). 

- The ephod mentioned here might not be the priestly garment. Some passages suggest an ephod could also be a statue ({{Judges 8:27|Judges 8:27}}; {{Judges 18:17|18:17}}).
Gath, a major Philistine city and the hometown of Goliath, was a clever but dangerous place for David to seek refuge from Saul.

*king of the land*: David’s reputation as a powerful warrior had become even greater than King Saul’s (see {{1 Samuel 18:7|1 Samuel 18:7}}). Because of this, people outside Israel began to speak of David as if he were already Israel’s king.

The long title of {{Psalm 34:1-22|Psalm 34}} mentions this event but calls the Philistine king Abimelech instead of Achish. "Abimelech" might have been a general title for Philistine kings (in Hebrew, it means "my father the king"). The name Abimelech also appears in {{Genesis 20:2|Genesis 20:2}} and {{Genesis 26:1|26:1}}.

- Adullam was about 25.8 kilometers (16 miles) southwest of Jerusalem, near Philistine land.

- If David's brothers and other relatives had stayed in Bethlehem, Saul could have easily targeted them for revenge.
Saul’s character is clear here. He could not take revenge on David himself. Instead, Saul killed those he believed had helped David.

*distressed … indebted … discontented*: The people who gathered around David were distressed, poor, and unhappy. By drawing such people to himself, David pointed ahead to Jesus, who would later welcome people who were hurting, burdened, and pushed to the edges of society ({{Matthew 11:25-30|Matthew 11:25–30}}).

- Mizpeh in Moab was east of the Dead Sea and the Jordan River. It was a difficult journey from Adullam, especially if David's 400 men traveled with him ({{1 Samuel 22:2|1 Samuel 22:2}}). 

- *they stayed with him*: Jesse's grandmother, Ruth, was a Moabite ({{Ruth 4:13-22|Ruth 4:13–22}}).
The prophet Gad was David’s special adviser ({{2 Samuel 24:11|2 Samuel 24:11}}). God had stopped communicating with Saul and was now guiding David.

*men of Benjamin*: Saul was suspicious of his own tribesmen. He believed David had paid them to be loyal to him. Worse, Saul did not even trust his own son. He believed his son was part of the supposed conspiracy.
David had deceived Ahimelech into thinking he was on a mission from Saul ({{1 Samuel 21:1-9|1 Samuel 21:1–9}}). Because of this, Saul’s accusations of conspiracy had no basis.
*the king’s son-in-law*: David had married Saul's daughter ({{1 Samuel 18:17-29|1 Samuel 18:17–29}}).

- *Doeg the Edomite … struck down the priests*: Doeg was not an Israelite, so he did not respect the holiness of priests chosen by God. He knew the priests were innocent, yet he still killed them. In this way, Doeg partly fulfilled God’s earlier judgment against the priestly family of Eli (see {{1 Samuel 2:27-34|1 Samuel 2:27–34}} and {{1 Kings 2:27|1 Kings 2:27}}).

- *men who wore the linen ephod*: This incident shows how irrational Saul had become. Not even those in sacred office were safe.

Saul had been unwilling to carry out God’s orders to destroy completely the Amalekites and their possessions ({{1 Samuel 15:3|1 Samuel 15:3}}, {{1 Samuel 15:9|9}}). Yet now, in his rage, he did not hesitate to destroy the priests' families and their possessions (see {{Proverbs 14:29|Proverbs 14:29}}; {{Proverbs 16:14|16:14}}; {{Proverbs 27:4|27:4}}).

Abiathar became an adviser to David, providing guidance from the Lord through the ephod (a priestly garment) ({{1 Samuel 23:2-12|1 Samuel 23:2–12}}; {{2 Samuel 15:24-36|2 Samuel 15:24–36}}). Later, he conspired with Adonijah against David and Solomon ({{1 Kings 1:1-2:46|1 Kings 1–2}}).
Keilah was near Adullam ({{1 Samuel 22:1|1 Samuel 22:1}}). It was at the western edge of Judah, near the Philistine border (see {{Joshua 15:44|Joshua 15:44}}; {{Nehemiah 3:17-18|Nehemiah 3:17–18}}).

Because Saul received reports from informants, he was able to continue pursuing David ({{1 Samuel 23:7|1 Samuel 23:7}},{{1 Samuel 23:13|13}}). David also had informants, which helped him stay ahead of Saul ({{1 Samuel 23:1|1 Samuel 23:1}}, {{1 Samuel 23:9|9}}, {{1 Samuel 23:15|15}}, {{1 Samuel 23:25|25}}). David’s greatest advantage was that he could seek guidance and help from God, which Saul did not have ({{1 Samuel 23:2|1 Samuel 23:2}}, {{1 Samuel 23:4|4}}, {{1 Samuel 23:12|12}}).

David asked the Lord for guidance, either by praying directly or by using the ephod (a priestly garment used to seek God’s will), as described in {{1 Samuel 23:6|1 Samuel 23:6}}, {{1 Samuel 23:9|9}}; {{2 Samuel 2:1|2 Samuel 2:1}}; and {{2 Samuel 5:23-24|2 Samuel 5:23–24}}. God’s answers were a sign of his blessing and protection (compare {{1 Samuel 28:6|1 Samuel 28:6}}).

*the ephod*: Saul killed 85 priests who wore ephods ({{1 Samuel 22:18|1 Samuel 22:18}}; see study note on 1 Samuel 2:18). However, the priest who escaped had the high priest's ephod, which held the Urim and Thummim (sacred objects used for decision-making).
*God has delivered him into my hand*: This statement is not true. David later explains that Saul’s claim is wrong (see {{1 Samuel 23:14|1 Samuel 23:14}}).

- The wilderness strongholds were natural rock formations that offered shelter. 

- Ziph was about 16 kilometers (10 miles) southeast of Keilah ({{1 Samuel 23:1|1 Samuel 23:1}}).
Jonathan encouraged David because he knew God had chosen David to be king.

*you will be king … I will be your second-in-command* (literally *second to you*): Jonathan accepted that God chose David as king and gave up his own ambitions to be king. Jonathan never held an official role in David’s court and died in battle with his father ({{1 Samuel 31:2|1 Samuel 31:2}}).

- *a covenant*: See {{1 Samuel 18:3-4|1 Samuel 18:3–4}}; {{1 Samuel 20:12-17|20:12–17}}. 

- *Jonathan went home*: This was likely the last time David and Jonathan saw each other.

- Hakilah was a hill in the wilderness region of Ziph ({{1 Samuel 23:14|1 Samuel 23:14}}). 

- Jeshimon is sometimes translated as “wasteland” rather than as a place name. Here, it refers to a specific wasteland north of the Dead Sea, on both banks of the Jordan River (see {{Numbers 21:20|Numbers 21:20}}).

Keilah ({{1 Samuel 23:12|1 Samuel 23:12}}) and Ziph ({{1 Samuel 23:14|23:14}}; {{Psalm 54:1|Psalm 54:1}}) were located in Judah, but neither one provided sanctuary for David, a native of Judah. David’s rise to power was not the result of his own tribe’s loyalty but because of the will of God.

- Maon was about 4.8 kilometers (3 miles) directly south of the wilderness of Ziph ({{1 Samuel 23:14|1 Samuel 23:14}}), about 16 kilometers (10 miles) south of Hebron. 

- The Arabah Valley is a deep rift stretching from above the Sea of Galilee down both sides of the Jordan River to the Dead Sea.

*Sela-hammahlekoth*: The Hebrew name is often translated "Rock of Escape." People in ancient Israel often gave place names to remember their thanks to God (for example, {{Genesis 22:14|Genesis 22:14}}; {{Genesis 28:19|28:19}}; {{Genesis 32:30|32:30}}). The exact rock formation that received this name is unknown.

David traveled eastward from the area of Ziph ({{1 Samuel 23:14|1 Samuel 23:14}}). He found safety in the strongholds of En-gedi. These rocky highlands were on the western shore of the Dead Sea. There was an oasis in this region, making it an ideal place to find water and food.

Saul chased David for a long time to try and kill him. Twice David had the opportunity to kill Saul. Both times his soldiers encouraged him to do it. But David respected Saul because God had chosen him to be Israel’s first king. David wouldn’t harm someone who was anointed to serve God.

But David did want to harm Nabal for treating him unkindly. David made a foolish and violent promise to kill all the men in Nabal’s household. Abigail was a wise and brave woman. Her words encouraged David not to kill his enemy. When Nabal died soon after, David wasn’t guilty of his death.
*three thousand chosen men*: David's force was outnumbered five to one ({{1 Samuel 23:13|1 Samuel 23:13}}).

- David’s men believed, as Saul did, that if the circumstances seem right, the Lord is telling you through those circumstances what to do (see {{1 Samuel 23:7|1 Samuel 23:7}}).

- David might have cut a piece of Saul’s robe without getting caught because Saul either took off the robe and set it aside or fell asleep in the cave.
David felt guilty because he had dishonored God's anointed king.

The Lord's anointed one was not to be harmed ({{1 Samuel 26:9|1 Samuel 26:9}}, {{1 Samuel 26:11|11}}, {{1 Samuel 26:16|16}}, {{1 Samuel 26:23|23}}; {{2 Samuel 1:14|2 Samuel 1:14}}, {{2 Samuel 1:16|16}}; {{2 Samuel 19:21|19:21}}). David refused to hurt Saul, even though God had chosen David to be the next king ({{1 Samuel 16:13|1 Samuel 16:13}}).

*my father*: Saul was actually David’s father-in-law ({{1 Samuel 18:27|1 Samuel 18:27}}). David was demonstrating his respect for the king and recalling a day when their relationship had been much friendlier.

- *May the LORD judge*: There was no human authority who could decide what was right between Saul and David. Because of this, David asked God to judge the matter (see {{Genesis 16:5|Genesis 16:5}}; {{Genesis 31:53|31:53}}; {{Exodus 5:21|Exodus 5:21}}; {{Judges 11:27|Judges 11:27}}). 

- *may the LORD take vengeance on you*: David trusted God's plan instead of trying to control it.
The proverb shows that David was in the right and that Saul was in the wrong. David refused to do evil, even when he had the chance to kill Saul. Saul, however, repeatedly tried to kill David.
*I know for sure that you will be king*: This was Saul's first open admission of the truth (compare {{1 Samuel 23:17|1 Samuel 23:17}}).

*swear to me … you will not cut off my descendants*: Having descendants was a way that Saul’s name would endure among the living. David had already sworn such an oath with Jonathan ({{1 Samuel 20:14-17|1 Samuel 20:14–17}}).

*Paran*: According to the Masoretic Text, David went to the wilderness of *Paran* after Samuel’s death. The Septuagint instead reads *Maon*, which fits better with the following story set in the Maon/Carmel area of Judah. This town in southern Judah (see study note on 1 Samuel 23:24) was probably Nabal’s home. The wilderness of Paran itself lay much farther south, in the northern Sinai near Kadesh-barnea, and is elsewhere described as a place of refuge ({{Genesis 21:21|Genesis 21:21}}; {{1 Kings 11:18|1 Kings 11:18}}).
This story about Nabal falls between two accounts in which Saul pursued David and David spared Saul’s life. Nabal was similar to Saul.

Carmel was a village near Maon. It should not be confused with the famous mountain from the story of Elijah in {{1 Kings 18:1-46|1 Kings 18}}. In this village, Saul built a monument to celebrate his victory over the Amalekites ({{1 Samuel 15:12|1 Samuel 15:12}}).

- *Nabal*: See {{1 Samuel 25:25|1 Samuel 25:25}} to understand the irony of his name. 

- Unlike her husband, Abigail was a sensible and wise person, as the story shows.
Sheep-shearing time for herdsmen was like harvest time for farmers. It was a time of celebration and thankfulness for blessings.

*son of Jesse*: This phrase refers to *David*. Like Saul, Nabal used this description in a disrespectful way. He avoided using David’s name to show contempt rather than honor ({{1 Samuel 20:27|1 Samuel 20:27}}, {{1 Samuel 20:31|31}}; {{1 Samuel 22:7|22:7}}).
*he has paid me back evil for good*: See also {{1 Samuel 24:17|1 Samuel 24:17}}.

*the LORD has held you back from bloodshed and from avenging yourself: Abigail* began her plea by saying that God had kept David from murder and revenge, and she ended it the same way ({{1 Samuel 25:31|1 Samuel 25:31}}). She reminded David that he had the power to kill Nabal, just as he had the power to kill Saul, but he chose not to do so.

- *a lasting dynasty*: God promised David that his family line would continue (see {{2 Samuel 7:1-29|2 Samuel 7}}).

- *fights the LORD’s battles*: David was famous and admired for defeating Israel’s enemies ({{1 Samuel 18:7|1 Samuel 18:7}}, {{1 Samuel 18:13|13}}, {{1 Samuel 18:16|16}}).

- *no evil be found in you*: This does not mean that David was without sin. It means that he was innocent in the way he pursued the throne. He did not try to seize it by violence, as {{1 Samuel 25:29-31|1 Samuel 25:29–31}} makes clear.

The phrase *like stones from a sling* fits David well. David famously defeated Goliath by striking him with a stone from a sling ({{1 Samuel 17:32-51|1 Samuel 17:32–51}}). The image reminds listeners of that event and highlights David’s strength and skill.
*for a king*: Nabal was like Saul (see study note on 1 Samuel 25:1–44).
Nabal was so stunned by the revelation that he had a stroke or a heart attack.

- Nabal’s death was God’s punishment for his sin. David could not be accused of vengeful murder.

- David quickly asked Abigail to marry him. She had proven herself wise and was also beautiful ({{1 Samuel 25:3|1 Samuel 25:3}}).

- Ahinoam was also the name of Saul’s wife ({{1 Samuel 14:50|1 Samuel 14:50}}). If she was the same woman, then David married Saul’s widow after Saul died ({{1 Samuel 31:1-13|1 Samuel 31:1–13}}). This would create another parallel between Nabal and Saul. However, other passages suggest they were two different women ({{1 Samuel 27:3|1 Samuel 27:3}}; {{1 Samuel 30:5|30:5}}). 

- This Jezreel was a small village in Judah, near Maon, Ziph, and Carmel ({{Joshua 15:55-56|Joshua 15:55–56}}). It was not the better-known northern city of Jezreel.
Saul likely gave Michal to another man for political reasons. He wanted to weaken David's claim to the throne by ending David's marriage to a royal family member.

- The men from Ziph had earlier offered to capture David and give him to Saul ({{1 Samuel 23:19-20|1 Samuel 23:19–20}}). 

- *Hakilah opposite Jeshimon*: The same place they had told Saul about before ({{1 Samuel 23:19|1 Samuel 23:19}}). David likely stayed nearby because the hilly area had many caves, which were good for hiding.

This was the last time Saul and David were together. The Ziphites informed Saul again about David's hiding place (see {{1 Samuel 23:19-20|1 Samuel 23:19–20}}). David spared Saul's life again, just like he did in the cave at En-gedi (see {{1 Samuel 24:1-22|1 Samuel 24}}).

Saul went after David again, even though he had earlier admitted that he was wrong ({{1 Samuel 24:17-21|1 Samuel 24:17–21}}). By this time, Saul was no longer able to think clearly or speak truthfully.
*Abner the son of Ner*: See study note on 1 Samuel 20:2.

- This is the only reference to Ahimelech the Hittite. 

- Zeruiah was David’s sister ({{1 Chronicles 2:16|1 Chronicles 2:16}}), making Abishai David’s nephew. Zeruiah's sons (Abishai, Joab, and Asahel) were three of David’s most loyal followers (for example, {{2 Samuel 2:18|2 Samuel 2:18}}). But they sometimes caused him trouble (see {{2 Samuel 3:39|2 Samuel 3:39}}; {{2 Samuel 16:10|16:10}}; {{2 Samuel 19:22|19:22}}).
*God has delivered your enemy into your hand*: Compare {{1 Samuel 24:4|1 Samuel 24:4}}.
*the LORD’s anointed*: See study note on 1 Samuel 24:6.

David was confident that God would judge between him and Saul just as he had done between him and Nabal (see {{1 Samuel 25:38|1 Samuel 25:38}}). Saul died in battle against the Philistines ({{1 Samuel 31:6|1 Samuel 31:6}}).
*deserve to die*: Death was the punishment for failing to do one's duty.
*Is that your voice, David my son?*: See {{1 Samuel 24:16|1 Samuel 24:16}}.

- *If the LORD has stirred you up against me*: David was confused by Saul’s actions and worried he might have sinned without knowing. 

- *if men have done it*: This might refer to Doeg ({{1 Samuel 22:9-10|1 Samuel 22:9–10}}). 

- *serve other gods*: This idea is similar to {{Psalm 137:4|Psalm 137:4}}. People exiled from the holy land could not worship the Lord through sacrifices at the main sanctuary.

- *I have sinned*: Saul had realized his mistakes before ({{1 Samuel 24:16-19|1 Samuel 24:16–19}}). David had no reason to trust him again (see {{1 Samuel 27:1|1 Samuel 27:1}}). 

- *I have played the fool*: The Hebrew word used here (*sakal*) means “to act foolishly” or “to play the fool” (see also {{1 Samuel 13:13|1 Samuel 13:13}}). This word is different from the word for “fool” (*nabal*) used in {{1 Samuel 25:1-44|1 Samuel 25}}. Even though the words are different, they have similar meanings. This helps show that Saul and Nabal are parallel figures. Both act foolishly and oppose God’s purposes.
David did not harm Saul ({{1 Samuel 24:6|1 Samuel 24:6}}; {{1 Samuel 26:9|26:9}}) because Saul was the Lord's anointed one (see study note on 1 Samuel 24:6).
*As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life*: David could not rely on Saul to do the same, so he trusted God with his fate.
Saul returned home, and this may have been David’s last personal encounter with him.
David fled to the Philistines to get away from Saul for good. Rather than killing Saul, David chose the dangerous life of a fugitive.

David and his men weren’t safe in Israel. A Philistine king gave them a town to live in. It was very hard for David not to live among the Israelites. Not being allowed to live in Israel was one of the covenant curses. Yet David was always faithful to God and worshipped only God.

Then the Amalekites destroyed David’s town. They captured David’s families’ and the families of his men. David and his soldiers were very sad and bitter about this. God helped them to get their families and belongings back. That happened while the Philistines went to attack the Israelites.

Saul was very afraid of the Philistine army. He tried to receive advice from God through dreams, prophets and casting lots. But he had refused to believe the words God had already told him through Samuel. Then he asked for help from a woman who was a medium. This means that she talked to spirits. She talked to the spiritual part of people whose bodies had died.

Samuel’s spirit told Saul the same things Samuel had told Saul before. Saul’s family line would no longer rule as kings. Saul, Jonathan and two of Saul’s other sons died in the battle against the Philistines. David was far away and wasn’t guilty of Saul’s death. After Saul died, the people of Jabesh Gilead honoured his body. They were the people Saul had rescued in his first battle as king.
This was David’s second stay with Achish, the Philistine king (see {{1 Samuel 21:10-15|1 Samuel 21:10–15}}). On both occasions, David lied to him (see {{1 Samuel 27:10|1 Samuel 27:10}}).

- Ziklag was about 35.4 kilometers (22 miles) southwest of Gath.

- *still belongs to the kings of Judah*: This note was written after Solomon’s death in 931 BC and before the beginning of the Babylonian exile in 586 BC.

- *the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites*: These groups lived on the edges of the southern desert and caused problems for both the Philistines and Israelites. (For more on the Amalekites, see {{1 Samuel 14:48|1 Samuel 14:48;}}{{1 Samuel 15:1-35|15}}; for more on the Geshurites, see {{Joshua 13:2|Joshua 13:2}}, {{Joshua 13:13|13}}; {{2 Samuel 3:3|2 Samuel 3:3}}.) 

- Shur was somewhere east of Egypt ({{1 Samuel 15:7|1 Samuel 15:7}}; {{Genesis 16:7|Genesis 16:7}}; {{Genesis 20:1|20:1}}; {{Genesis 25:18|25:18}}).

*he did not leave a man or woman alive*: At least some of these people were among those whom God had commanded Israel to destroy (see {{1 Samuel 15:3|1 Samuel 15:3}}; {{1 Samuel 28:18|28:18}}; {{Deuteronomy 25:17-19|Deuteronomy 25:17–19}}; {{Joshua 13:13|Joshua 13:13}}).

- David misled Achish by claiming his attacks were against his own people of Judah and two other related groups. The text neither praises nor criticizes David for lying to the foreign king.

- The Jerahmeelites were a Semitic tribe (an ancient people group from the Middle East who shared related languages and customs) living in southern Judah (see {{1 Chronicles 2:9|1 Chronicles 2:9}}, {{1 Chronicles 2:25-27|25–27}}, {{1 Chronicles 2:33|33}}, {{1 Chronicles 2:42|42}}). 

- *Kenites*: The father-in-law of Moses was a Kenite (see {{Judges 1:16|Judges 1:16}}; {{Judges 4:11|4:11}}; see also study note on 1 Samuel 15:6).
*for warfare*: Fights between Israel and the Philistines happened often. In exchange for providing refuge, Achish expected David’s military involvement and cooperation.

*had removed … from the land*: Saul had either forced most mediums (people who claimed they could communicate with the spirits of the dead) to leave the land or put them to death. Or he had made necromancy (the practice of trying to speak with the dead) illegal (see study note on 1 Samuel 28:9).
Saul consulted the dead, a practice forbidden by God’s law (see {{Leviticus 20:27|Leviticus 20:27}}; {{Deuteronomy 18:9-11|Deuteronomy 18:9–11}}).

- Shunem was a border town in the land of Issachar ({{Joshua 19:18|Joshua 19:18}}). It overlooked the Valley of Jezreel. 

- Mount Gilboa is at the east end of the Valley of Jezreel. The mountain got its name from a nearby village.

*did not answer him*: Earlier, Saul had asked the Lord for guidance using sacred lots, but the results were unclear ({{1 Samuel 14:36-42|1 Samuel 14:36–42}}). God's silence was a sign of his judgment ({{1 Samuel 14:37|1 Samuel 14:37}}; {{Lamentations 2:9|Lamentations 2:9}}; {{Ezekiel 7:26|Ezekiel 7:26}}; {{Amos 8:11-12|Amos 8:11–12}}; {{Micah 3:6-7|Micah 3:6–7}}).

- Without God's guidance, Saul turned to forbidden ways to learn God's will. Saul had earlier banned the occult practice that he now used himself ({{1 Samuel 28:3|1 Samuel 28:3}}). 

- Endor was on the border between Israel and Philistia. The area near Israel’s border was probably a safer location for a banned practice.
*killed*: Literally *cut off,* suggesting that Saul might have had most of the mediums executed.
We do not know why seeing Samuel caused this woman to recognize Saul.

Saul asked the medium to describe what she saw that caused her to scream. She described a divine being, a god (Hebrew *’elohim*) coming up. erhaps she observed a human figure with a godlike or angelic appearance, or her use of the term *god* might reflect a pagan belief that a person becomes *a god *(a spirit possessing supernatural abilities) after death.

- *God has turned away from me*: The same Hebrew term appears in {{1 Samuel 16:14|1 Samuel 16:14}} and {{Judges 16:20|Judges 16:20}}. 

- *no longer answers me, either by prophets or by dreams*: Compare {{1 Samuel 28:6|1 Samuel 28:6}}.
Saul’s enemy was not David but the Lord himself.
*torn the kingship out of your hand*: See {{1 Samuel 15:28|1 Samuel 15:28}}.
*you did not obey*: Samuel's message to Saul had not changed (compare {{1 Samuel 15:19|1 Samuel 15:19}}).

*will be with me*: In *Sheol*, the place where the dead are believed to dwell (compare {{1 Samuel 2:6|1 Samuel 2:6}}, *to Sheol*; see also {{Numbers 16:30-33|Numbers 16:30–33}}; {{Job 17:1-16|Job 17:1–16}}; {{Psalm 49:11|Psalm 49:11}}; {{Revelation 1:18|Revelation 1:18}}).

*fattened calf … flour … and baked unleavened bread*: Preparing this meal required much time and effort. It showed generous hospitality (compare {{Genesis 18:5-7|Genesis 18:5–7}}). The meal that the medium shared with Saul recalls the fine meal that Samuel once shared with Saul ({{1 Samuel 9:22-24|1 Samuel 9:22–24}}). That earlier meal, shared with God’s prophet, marked the beginning of Saul’s kingship. This later meal, shared with a condemned medium, came shortly before Saul’s death.

- Aphek was the site of an earlier confrontation between Israel and the Philistines ({{1 Samuel 4:1|1 Samuel 4:1}}). 

- Jezreel was about 64.4 kilometers (40 miles) northeast of Aphek.
God's help saved David from having to fight his own people.

- *the servant of King Saul of Israel*: To Achish, David appeared to be a valuable defector (someone who had left his former king). The other Philistine rulers were suspicious. They feared that David was a spy who planned to attack them from inside their defenses.

- *found no fault in him*: This was the first of three times Achish defended David (see also {{1 Samuel 29:6|1 Samuel 29:6}}, {{1 Samuel 29:9|9}}). However, David had been deceiving Achish the entire time (see {{1 Samuel 27:1-12|1 Samuel 27:1–12}}).
*with the heads of our men*: The commanders' fears were justified (compare {{1 Samuel 17:51|1 Samuel 17:51}}; {{1 Samuel 18:27|18:27}}).
This *song* referred to Philistines whom David had killed ({{1 Samuel 18:7|1 Samuel 18:7}}). Because of this, it is surprising that David was able to find safety among them.

- *as the LORD*: Achish used the unique name of Israel’s God to prove his own sincerity. 

- *no fault in you*: This statement was not completely true, but Achish did not realize this ({{1 Samuel 27:8-12|1 Samuel 27:8–12}}).

- *Ziklag*: See study note on 1 Samuel 27:6. 

- The Amalekites might have been striking back because David raided them ({{1 Samuel 27:8|1 Samuel 27:8}}).

- There were no soldiers left in Ziklag to protect the women and children. The Amalekites were known for attacking the weak and vulnerable (see {{Deuteronomy 25:17-18|Deuteronomy 25:17–18}}). 

- *not killed anyone*: The Amalekites were not being kind. They found women and children more valuable alive than dead.

- *Ahinoam*: See the study note on 1 Samuel 25:43. 

- *Abigail*: See {{1 Samuel 25:3-42|1 Samuel 25:3–42}}.

*greatly distressed*: Saul had used the same expression about himself. When he was *in *deep trouble, Saul turned to necromancy (trying to speak with the dead). This led to disaster ({{1 Samuel 28:15|1 Samuel 28:15}}). David, in contrast, found strength and success in the Lord his God.
*the ephod*: See study notes on 1 Samuel 2:18 and 23:6.

Unlike Saul ({{1 Samuel 28:6|1 Samuel 28:6}}), David successfully asked the Lord for guidance (see {{1 Samuel 23:9-12|1 Samuel 23:9–12}}; {{2 Samuel 2:1|2 Samuel 2:1}}; {{2 Samuel 5:19|5:19}}, {{2 Samuel 5:23|23}}).
Besor was a large stream in Philistine territory. It flowed into the Mediterranean Sea southwest of Gaza.

*too exhausted*: David's men were very tired after traveling for three days ({{1 Samuel 30:1|1 Samuel 30:1}}). They were now chasing the Amalekites without having rested. David did not scold them or force them to keep going without mercy. See {{1 Samuel 30:23-25|1 Samuel 30:23–25}}.
David once received bread when he was very hungry ({{1 Samuel 21:3-7|1 Samuel 21:3–7}}). He and his men helped this Egyptian man before knowing who he was or if he could assist them.
*when I fell ill*: The Amalekites valued only slaves who were healthy and strong. They considered the others useless and left them behind.
The land of Caleb was in the wilderness of Judah, south of Hebron (see {{Joshua 14:6-15|Joshua 14:6–15}}).
The total number of Amalekite raiders must have been quite large if 400 young men escaped.
*he greeted them*: David did not scold them for not participating in the battle.
David generously divided the spoils among those who participated in the battle and those who were too exhausted to take part.
*They may take them and go*: This unkind group wanted to send away those who had not taken part, without giving them any reward.
*what the LORD has given us*: Some of David's men believed their success came from their own military skills. David attributed victory to God and gave him the glory.
*They will share alike*: Compare with {{Numbers 31:25-47|Numbers 31:25–47}}, where Moses divided the plunder of war between those who fought and the rest of the people.
*his friends, the elders of Judah*: David extended his generosity to influential people throughout his own tribal area, possibly to secure their support for him as king.
The places mentioned here were all in southern Judah. David eventually emerged from this territory as king (see {{2 Samuel 2:1-4|2 Samuel 2:1–4}}).
David ruled as king over Judah from the city of Hebron for seven and a half years ({{2 Samuel 2:1-7|2 Samuel 2:1–7}}; {{2 Samuel 5:5|5:5}}).

- The Israelites fled southeast from the Valley of Jezreel ({{1 Samuel 29:1|1 Samuel 29:1}}) to higher and hillier areas. With their chariots, the Philistines had the advantage in the more level valley. 

- Mount Gilboa is southwest of the Sea of Galilee, far from the territory of the Philistines.
While David was in the south successfully fighting the Amalekites ({{1 Samuel 30:1-31|1 Samuel 30}}), Saul was in the north unsuccessfully fighting the Philistines.
*Jonathan … Malkishua*: See {{1 Samuel 14:49|1 Samuel 14:49}}. This is the first mention of Saul’s son Abinadab (compare {{1 Chronicles 8:33|1 Chronicles 8:33}}; {{1 Chronicles 9:39|9:39}}).

- David had earlier served as an armor bearer (a personal assistant who carried a soldier’s weapons) to Saul ({{1 Samuel 16:21|1 Samuel 16:21}}). 

- *run me through*: This is one of many similarities between the death of Abimelech during the time of the judges ({{Judges 9:1-57|Judges 9}}) and Saul, Israel’s first national king (see {{Judges 9:54|Judges 9:54}}). In both stories, a wounded leader asks someone else to kill him rather than die in shame.
After a victory, the army would remove items from the dead. They searched the bodies for anything valuable, such as clothing, weapons, or jewelry.

In the ancient world, people saw the death of an enemy king as good news. They believed it meant that the enemy’s god had been defeated. The Philistines did not realize that their victory would not last and would bring them no real gain. David, the Lord’s true anointed king, would soon come to power and defeat the Philistines. Instead of defeating Israel’s God, the Philistines were unknowingly carrying out his purpose.

- *the Ashtoreths*: See {{1 Samuel 7:3|1 Samuel 7:3}}.

- *hung his body*: This act further humiliated the executed person by denying them a proper burial. It also served as a warning to other potential enemies (see also {{Genesis 40:19|Genesis 40:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 21:21-22|Deuteronomy 21:21–22}}; {{Joshua 10:26|Joshua 10:26}}; {{Esther 9:6-14|Esther 9:6–14}}). 

- Beth-shan was a short distance east of Mount Gilboa.

The people of Jabesh-gilead were repaying a kindness. Earlier, Saul had rescued them from the Ammonites and their king Nahash ({{1 Samuel 11:1-13|1 Samuel 11:1–13}}). Jabesh-gilead was about nineteen kilometers (twelve miles) southeast of Beth-shan. It lay across the Jordan River.
*burned the bodies*: Cremation was uncommon in the ancient world. The bodies may have been burned because decomposition had already begun.

- *bones … Jabesh*: This was not where Saul's remains were finally laid to rest (see {{2 Samuel 21:12-14|2 Samuel 21:12–14}}).

- The end of 1 Samuel returns Israel's history to the time at the end of Judges, when “Israel had no king.” The Philistines were in control again. David had God’s anointing but no crown. He had wives but no sons. His connection with the hated Philistines may have put his standing with his own people at risk. David's future would be difficult. Still, it was clear that God was with him.

1:1: There was a certain man of Ramah, of the pupils of the prophets, of the hill country of the House of Ephraim, whose name was Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, a man having a portion in the holy things in the hill country of the House of Ephraim.
1:2: And he had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah. And Peninnah had sons, but Hannah had no sons.
1:3: And that man used to go up from his city, periodically from festival to festival, to bow down and to sacrifice before the LORD Sebaoth at Shiloh, where the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinahas, were serving before the LORD.
1:4: And on the festival when Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters.
1:5: And he would give to Hannah one choice portion, because he loved Hannah. And from before the LORD offspring was withheld from her.
1:6: And her rival used to provoke her, also to anger her in order to make her jealous, because from before the LORD offspring was withheld from her.
1:7: And so he did year by year; as often as she went up to the house of the LORD’s sanctuary, she used to anger her. And she was weeping and would not eat.
1:8: And Elkanah, her husband, said to her, ‘Hannah, why are you weeping? And why did you not eat? And why is your heart sad to you? Is not my goodwill better to you than ten sons?’
1:9: And Hannah rose, after she had eaten in Shiloh and after they had drunk. Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat beside the doorpost of the LORD’s temple.
1:10: And she was bitter of soul and she prayed before the LORD and wept abundantly.
1:11: And she swore an oath and said, ‘O LORD Sebaoth, the affliction of thy maidservant is indeed revealed before Thee. And let my memory come in before Thee and do not keep thy maidservant far away. And give to thy maidservant a son in the midst of the sons of men. And I will hand him over, that he may serve before the LORD all the days of his life. And the dominion of man will not be upon him.’
1:12: And when she continued praying before the LORD, Eli was waiting for her until she would stop.
1:13: And Hannah was praying in her heart. Only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard. And Eli took her to be as a drunken woman.
1:14: And Eli said to her, ‘How long will you act insane? Will you not let your wine evaporate from you?’
1:15: And Hannah answered and said, ‘No, my lord, I am a woman anguished of spirit. I have drunk neither new nor old wine, but I have told the humiliation of my soul in prayer before the LORD.
1:16: Do not rebuke your maidservant as a daughter of wickedness, for from the abundance of my jealousy and my anger I lingered in prayer until now.’
1:17: And Eli answered and said, ‘Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant you your petition which you have made from before Him.’
1:18: And she said, ‘Let your maidservant find favour in your sight.’ Then the woman went her way and ate, and her countenance was no longer sad.
1:19: They rose early in the morning and bowed down before the LORD. Then they went back to their house, to Ramah. And Elkanah knew his wife Hannah and her memory went in before the LORD.
1:20: And at the time of the completing of the days Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called him name Samuel, for she said, ‘I have asked him from before the LORD.’
1:21: And the man Elkanah and all the people of his house went up to sacrifice before the LORD the sacrifice of the festival, and to fulfil his vow.
1:22: But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, ‘As soon as the boy is weaned, I will bring him that he be seen before the LORD and live there for ever.’
1:23: And her husband Elkanah said to her, ‘Do what seems right in your sight; wait until you have weaned him. Only, may the LORD establish his words.’ So the woman waited and nursed her son, until she weaned him.
1:24: And when she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with three bulls, one measure of flour and a skin of wine; and she brought him to the sanctuary of the LORD, to Shiloh. And the boy was young.
1:25: And they slaughtered the bull and brought the boy to Eli.
1:26: And she said, ‘Please, my lord! By your life, my lord, I am the woman who was standing here with you to pray before the LORD.
1:27: Concerning this boy I prayed; and the LORD granted me my petition which I made from before Him.
1:28: And I have als handed him over that he may be serving before the LORD. All the days that he lives, he will serve before the LORD.’ And he bowed down before the LORD there.
2:1: And Hannah prayed in a prophetic spirit and said, ‘Now my son Samuel is to be a prophet over Israel. 3:12: On that day I will fulfil against Eli all that I have spoken concerning the people of his house. I will destroy and I will end.
3:13: And I told him that I take revenge on the people of his house for ever, for the sins which he knew, because his sons are provoking and he did not restrain them.
3:14: Therefore, I swore to the house of Eli that the sins of Eli’s house shall not be forgiven by holy slaughterings or offerings for ever.’
3:15: And Samuel lay until morning; then he opened the doors of the sanctuary of the LORD. And Samuel was afraid to tell the prophetic vision to Eli.
3:16: But Eli called Samuel and said, ‘Samuel, my son.’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’
3:17: And he said, ‘What is the word that He spoke with you? Do not hide it from me. May the LORD do so to you and more also, if you hide anything from me of all the word that He spoke with you.’
3:18: So Samuel told him all the words and hid nothing from him. And he said, ‘It is the LORD; let him do what is right before Him.’
3:19: And Samuel grew, and the speech of the LORD was in his aid, and none of all his words failed.
3:20: And all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was reliable in the prophetic words of the LORD.
3:21: And the LORD continued to reveal himself at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.
4:1: And the word of Samuel was pleasing to all Israel. Now Israel went out to wage war against the Philistines; they encamped at Stone of Help and the Philistines encamped at Aphek.
4:2: The Philistines drew up in line against Israel, and when the wagers of the battle spread, Israel was shattered before the Philistines. They slew about four thousand men in the battle line on the field.
4:3: And when the people came to the camp, the elders of Israel said, “Why has the LORD shattered us today before the Philistines? Let us take the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Shiloh to us, that he may go between us. On account of the Glory of his name we will be saved from the hand of our enemies.”
4:4: So the people sent to Shiloh, and they carried from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD Sebaoth, whose Presence dwells above the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of the LORD.
4:5: When the ark of the covenant of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave a mighty shout, so that the earth resounded.
4:6: And when the Philistines heard the noise of the shouting, they said, “What is this noise of a great shouting in the camp of the Judaeans?” And they learned that the ark of the LORD had come to the camp.
4:7: And the Philistines were afraid, for they said, “The ark of the LORD has come to the camp.” And they said, “Woe to us! For it was not like this yesterday and before that.
4:8: Woe to us! Who can deliver us from the hand of the speech of the LORD, whose works are great? These are the mighty deeds of the LORD, who smote the Egyptians with every plague, but did for his people wonders in the wilderness.
4:9: Take courage and be heroic men, O Philistines, lest you become subjected to the Judaeans as they have been subjected to you. Be heroic men and wage war!”
4:10: And the Philistines did wage war. And Israel was shattered, and they retreated, every man to his city. And it was a very great slaughter, and there fell of Israel thirty thousand foot soldiers.
4:11: And the ark of the LORD was captured; and the two sons of Eli were killed, Hophni and Phinehas.
4:12: And a man from the tribe of Benjamin’s House ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and earth thrown upon his head.
4:13: When he came, behold, Eli was sitting upon his seat on the path of the gateway, on the look out, for his heart trembled for the ark of the LORD. And when the man came to tell [the news] in the city, all the city was shaken.
4:14: When Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he said, “What is the sound of this panic?” Then the man hastened and came to tell Eli.
4:15: Now Eli was ninety eight years old and his eyes were set, so that he could not see.
4:16: And the man said to Eli, “I came from the battle line, and I fled from the battle line today.” And he said, “What was the situation, my son?”
4:17: He who brought the tidings answered and said, “Israel has retreated from before the Philistines, and there has also been a great stroke among the people; your two sons also, Hophni and Phinehas, have been killed and the ark of the LORD has been captured.”
4:18: When he mentioned the ark of the LORD, Eli fell backward from his seat on the path of the gateway; and his neck was broken and he died, for he was an old man, and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years.
4:19: Now his daughter in law, the wife of Phinehas, was with child, about to give birth. And when she heard the report that the ark of the LORD was captured, and that her father in law had died, and that her husband was killed, she bowed and gave birth, for her pains frightened her.
4:20: And about the time of her death the women standing around her said to her, “Fear not, for you have borne a male son.” But she did not answer or give heed.
4:21: And she named the boy Ichabod, saying, “The Glory has been exiled from Israel!” for the ark of the LORD had been captured and her father in law had died and her husband had been killed.
4:22: She had said, “The Glory has been exiled from Israel,” for the ark of the Lord has been captured.
5:1: When the Philistines captured the ark of the LORD, they brought it from the Stone of Help to Ashdod.
5:2: Then the Philistines took the ark of the LORD and brought it into the house of Dagon and set it up beside Dagon.
5:3: And when the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen on his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place.
5:4: When they rose early in the morning the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen on his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD. And the head of Dagon and the two palms of his hands were lying cut off upon the threshold; only his body was left to him.
5:5: Therefore the idol priests of Dagon and all who enter the house of Dagon do not tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day.
5:6: And the stroke of the LORD was heavily upon the people of Ashdod, and He terrified and afflicted them with haemorrhoids, both Ashdod and its territory.
5:7: And when the people of Ashdod saw that the stroke was equally upon them, they said, “The ark of the God of Israel must not dwell with us; for his stroke is heavily upon us and upon Dagon our idol.”
5:8: So they sent and gathered together all the chiefs of the Philistines, and said, “What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” They said, “Let the ark of the God of Israel be brought around to Gath.” So they brought the ark of the God of Israel around.
5:9: But after they had brought it around, the stroke of the LORD was on the city, a very great panic. And He struck the men of the city, great and small, so that they were afflicted with haemorrhoids.
5:10: So they sent the ark of the LORD to Ekron. And when the ark of the LORD came to Ekron, the Ekronites cried out, “They have brought around to me the ark of the God of Israel to kill us and our people.”
5:11: Then they sent and gathered together all the chiefs of the Philistines, and said, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its own place, that it may not kill me and my people.” For there was a deathly panic throughout the whole city. The stroke of the LORD was very heavy there.
5:12: The men who did not die were stricken with haemorrhoids, and the cry of the city went up toward heaven.
6:1: And the ark of the LORD was in the cities of the Philistines seven months.
6:2: And the Philistines called for the priests and the diviners, saying, “What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Let us know with what we shall send it to its place.”
6:3: And they said, “If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty, for you shall by all means return before Him a guilt offering. Then you will be healed and it will be relieved to you. Why would his stroke not rest from you?”
6:4: When they said, “What is the guilt offering that we shall return before Him?” they said, “The number of the chiefs of the Philistines: five golden haemorrhoids and five golden mice, for the one stroke was equally on all of you and on your chiefs.
6:5: So you must make images of your haemorrhoids and images of your mice that ravaged the land, and you shall give glory before the God of Israel. Perhaps his stroke will rest from you and your idols and your land.
6:6: Why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and the pharaoh hardened their hearts? Was that not when revenge was taken on them? And afterwards they sent them away and they went.
6:7: Now then, take and prepare one new cart and two milch cows which have never pulled in a yoke. And bind the cows to the cart, but send their calves back inside, so that they cannot follow them.
6:8: And you shall take the ark of the LORD and put it down on the cart. And you shall place in a box at its side the golden figures which you are returning before Him as a guilt offering. Then you shall send it off, and it will go.
6:9: And you shall watch: if it goes up on the way of its own territory, to Beth shemesh, then this great harm was done from before Him; but if not, then we shall know that it was not his stroke that came near to us, it happened to us by chance.”
6:10: And the men did so, and led two milch cows and bound them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home.
6:11: And they put the ark of the LORD on the cart, and the box and the golden mice and the images of their haemorrhoids.
6:12: And the cows went straight on the way, in the direction of Beth shemesh, along one highway, lowing as they went. They turned neither to the right nor to the left, and the chiefs of the Philistines went after them as far as the border of Beth shemesh.
6:13: And Beth shemesh was harvesting the wheat harvest in the valley; and when they lifted up their eyes and saw the ark, they rejoiced to see it.
6:14: The cart went to the field of Joshua, who was of Beth shemesh, and stood there. And a great stone was there; and they split up the wood of the cart and sacrificed the cows as a burnt offering before the LORD.
6:15: And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the box that was with it, in which were the golden things, and put them upon the great stone. And the men of Beth shemesh sacrificed burnt offerings and slaughtered holy sacrifices on that day before the LORD.
6:16: And when the five chiefs of the Philistines saw it, they returned that day to Ekron.
6:17: These are the golden haemorrhoids which the Philistines returned as a guilt offering before the LORD: one of Ashdod, one of Gaza, one of Ashkelon, one of Gath, one of Ekron.
6:18: And the golden mice, the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five chiefs, from the fortified cities unto the unwalled cities, and unto the great stone on which they returned the ark of the LORD, to this day. Behold, it is in the field of Joshua who was of Beth shemesh.
6:19: And He killed among the men of Beth shemesh, because they rejoiced as they saw the ark of the LORD, when it was exposed; and He killed among the elders of the people seventy men and among the assembly fifty thousand men. And the people mourned, because the LORD had made a great stroke among the people.
6:20: Then the men of Beth shemesh said, “Who is able to stand before the ark of the LORD, this holy God? And to what place shall it be brought up, away from us?”
6:21: So they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath jearim, saying, “The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to you.”
7:1: And the men of Kiriath jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD and brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill and they appointed his son, Eleazar, to guard the ark of the LORD.
7:2: From the day that the ark lodged in Kiriath jearim many days passed – it became twenty years – and all the House of Israel gathered themselves after the worship of the LORD.
7:3: Then Samuel said to all the house of Israel, “If you are returning to the worship of the LORD with all your heart, then remove the idols of the nations and the Ashtaroth from among you, and direct your heart to the worship of the LORD and worship before Him alone. And He will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines.”
7:4: So Israel removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth and they worshipped before the LORD alone.
7:5: Then Samuel said, “Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray before the LORD on behalf of you.”
7:6: So they gathered themselves at Mizpah, and poured out their hearts like water, in repentance before the LORD. And they fasted on that day, and said there, “We are guilty before the LORD.” And Samuel judged the sons of Israel at Mizpah.
7:7: When the Philistines heard that the sons of Israel had gathered themselves at Mizpah, the chiefs of the Philistines went up against Israel. And when the sons of Israel heard of it, they feared before the Philistines.
7:8: And the sons of Israel said to Samuel, “Do not fall silent in your prayer for us before the LORD our God, that He may save us from the hand of the Philistines.”
7:9: So Samuel took one sucking lamb and sacrificed it as a whole burnt offering before the LORD. And Samuel prayed before the LORD on behalf of Israel and the LORD accepted his prayer.
7:10: As Samuel was sacrificing up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to wage war against Israel. But the LORD thundered with a great voice that day against the Philistines and confused them; and they were shattered before Israel.
7:11: And the men of Israel went out of Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, and smote them, as far as below Beth sharon.
7:12: Then Samuel took one stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name “Stone of Help”, for he said, “Up to here the LORD has helped us.”
7:13: So the Philistines were shattered and did not again cross the border of the land of Israel. And the stroke of the LORD was on the Philistines all the days of Samuel.
7:14: The cities which the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron to Gath; and Israel delivered them from the hand of the Philistines. And there was peace between Israel and the Amorites.
7:15: Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.
7:16: And he used to go on a circuit year by year to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah; and he was judging Israel, all these places.
7:17: And on his return to Ramah – for there was his house and there he judged Israel – he built there an altar before the LORD.
8:1: When Samuel became old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
8:2: The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of his second Abijah; they were judges in Beersheba.
8:3: Yet his sons did not walk in his ways, but turned aside after false riches. They accepted bribes and perverted justice.
8:4: Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah.
8:5: And they said to him, “Behold, you have become old and your sons do not walk in your ways; now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations.”
8:6: But the thing was evil in Samuel’s sight, when they said, “Appoint for us a king to judge us.” And Samuel prayed before the LORD.
8:7: And the LORD said to Samuel, “Accept the speech of the people in all that they say to you, for it is not you they have rejected, for they have refused my worship so that I cannot be king over them anymore.
8:8: According to all the deeds which they have done, from the day I brought them up out of Egypt to this day – they have forsaken my worship and have worshipped the idols of the nations so they are also doing to you, too.
8:9: Now then, accept their speech. Only, you shall solemnly warn them, and tell them the right of the king who shall reign over them.”
8:10: So Samuel told all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking a king from him.
8:11: He said, “This is the right of the king who shall reign over you: he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to be his horsemen and the pursuers before his chariots;
8:12: and to appoint for himself commanders of thousands and commanders of fifty; and farmers to plough his ground and to reap his harvest; and craftsmen to make his implements of war and the equipment for his chariots.
8:13: He will take your daughters to be servants and cooks and bakers.
8:14: He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive orchards and give them to his servants.
8:15: He will take one tenth of your grain and of your vineyards and give it to his commanders and his servants.
8:16: The most handsome of your menservants, your maidservants, your young men and your asses he will take for his business.
8:17: He will take one tenth of your flocks, and you will be his servants.
8:18: And in that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not accept your prayer in that day.”
8:19: But the people rebelled against accepting Samuel’s speech and they said, “No! but there will be a king over us.
8:20: Then also we will be like all the nations. Our king will avenge us and go out at our head and wage our wars.”
8:21: And when Samuel had heard all the words of the people, he reported them before the LORD.
8:22: And the LORD said to Samuel, “Accept the speech of the people and make them a king.” Samuel then said to the men of Israel, “Go, every man to his city.”
9:1: There was a man of the tribe of the House of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, son of a man from the tribe of the House of Benjamin, a mighty hero.
9:2: And he had a son whose name was Saul, a handsome young man. There was not a man among the sons of Israel who was more handsome than he. From his shoulder upward he was taller than all the people.
9:3: Now the asses of Kish, Saul’s father, were lost. So Kish said to Saul his son, “Take one of the servants with you, and arise, go in search of the asses.”
9:4: And he passed through the hill country of the House of Ephraim and passed through the land of the South, but they did not find them. And they passed through the Land of the Birth stool, but they were not there. Then he passed through the land of Benjamin, but they did not find them.
9:5: When they came to the land in which there was a prophet, Saul said to his young man, who was with him, “Come, let us go back, lest my father leave the matter of the asses and become anxious about us.”
9:6: But he said to him, “Behold now, there is a prophet of the LORD in this city, and he is a man prophesying the truth; all that he prophesies will certainly be fulfilled. Now then, let us go there; perhaps he can tell us about our ways on which we have gone.”
9:7: Then Saul said to his young man, “Suppose we go, if he isused to accepting money, what can we bring the prophet of the LORD Moreover, our own provision ceased from our sacks, and there is nothing fit to bring to the prophet of the LORD What is there with us to do?”
9:8: And again the servant answered Saul, “Behold, I have in my hand one silver zuz, and I can give it to the prophet of the LORD, that he may tell us our way.”
9:9: Formerly in Israel, when a man went to seek instruction from before the LORD he said it like this, “Come and let us meet the seer.” For he who is called a prophet today was formerly called a seer.
9:10: And Saul said to his young man, “Your word is right; come, let us go.” So they went to the city where the prophet of the LORD was.
9:11: As they went up by the ascent of the city, they met young women coming out to draw water, and said to them, “Is the seer here?”
9:12: They answered them and said, “He is here, just ahead of you. Make haste, for today he has entered the city, because there is a meal with the holy slaughterings for the people today in the banqueting hall.
9:13: As soon as you enter the city, you will find him, before he goes up to the banqueting hall to eat; for the people will not eat till he comes, since he [always] says the benediction over the food; afterward those eat who are invited. Now, go up, for you can find him at this time.”
9:14: So they went up to the city. As they were entering the city, behold, Samuel was coming out toward them on his way up to the banqueting hall.
9:15: And from before the LORD it was said to Samuel, one day before Saul’s coming,
9:16: “Tomorrow about this time I will send to you a man from the land of the tribe of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be king over my people Israel. He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines, for the oppression of my people is revealed before Me, for their complaint has come before Me.”
9:17: When Samuel saw Saul, from before the LORD it was said to him, “Behold, the man of whom I spoke to you. He is it who will take away the dominion from my people.”
9:18: Then Saul met Samuel in the gate, and said, “Tell me where is the house of the seer?”
9:19: Samuel answered Saul, “I am the seer; go up before me to the banqueting hall. Today you shall eat with me, and in the morning I will let you go and tell you all that is on your mind.
9:20: As for the matter of the asses that were lost to you, and which you came to search – today for three days – do not set your mind on them, for they have been found. But whose is all the delight of Israel? Is it not yours and all the house of your father?”
9:21: Saul answered, “Am I not a son of the tribe of Benjamin, from the least of the tribes of Israel? And is not my family the weakest of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken with me in this way?”
9:22: Then Samuel led Saul and his young man and brought them to the meal and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited, who were about thirty persons.
9:23: And Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion I gave to you, of which I said to you, ‘Keep it with you.’”
9:24: So the cook took up the shank and the loin and set them before Saul. And he said, “See, what was left over is set before you. Eat, for it was kept for you for the time [I would] say, ‘I have invited the people to the meal.’” So Saul ate with Samuel on that day.
9:25: When they came down from the banqueting hall into the city, he spoke with Saul on the roof.
9:26: And they got up early. Then at the break of dawn Samuel called to Saul upon the roof, “Rise up, and I will send you off.” So Saul arose, and both he and Samuel went outside.
9:27: As they were going down to the outskirts of the city, Samuel said to Saul, “Say to your young man that he must pass on before us,” – and he passed on – “And you, stand here this moment, that I may make you hear the word of the LORD.”
10:1: Then Samuel took a vessel of oil and poured it on his head, and he kissed him and said, “Has not the LORD anointed you to be the king over his inheritance?”
10:2: When you depart from me today, you will find two men by Rachel’s tomb in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah, and they will say to you, “The asses which you went to seek are found, and now your father has left off the matter of the asses and is anxious about you, saying, ‘What shall I do about my son?’”
10:3: Then you shall go on from there further, and come to the valley of Tabor; three men who are going up to bow down before the LORD at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three kids, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine.
10:4: And they will ask you about your well being and give you two loaves of wreathed bread, which you shall accept from their hand.
10:5: After that you shall go to the hill where the ark of the LORD is, where the praetors of the Philistines are. And there, as you come to the city, you will meet a company of scribes coming down from the banqueting hall and before them harps, tambourines, cymbals and lyres, and they will be praising.
10:6: Then a prophetic spirit from before the LORD will dwell upon you, and you shall praise with them and be turned into another man.
10:7: When these signs will come to you, prepare for yourselves the instruments of kingship, for the speech of the LORD is in your aid.
10:8: And you shall go down before me to Gilgal; and behold, I am coming down to you to sacrifice burnt offerings and to slaughter holy slaughterings. Seven days you shall wait, until I come to you and tell you what you shall do.”
10:9: And when he turned away from Samuel, the LORD gave him another heart. And all these signs came to pass that day.
10:10: When they came there, to the hill, behold, a company of scribes met them; and a prophetic spirit from before the LORD dwelt upon him, and he praised among them.
10:11: And when all who knew him before saw that he was praising among the scribes, the people said, one to another, “What is this that has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the scribes?”
10:12: And a man from there answered, and said, “And who is their master?” Therefore it became a proverb, “Is Saul also among the scribes?”
10:13: When he had finished praising, he entered the banqueting hall.
10:14: Saul’s uncle said to him and to his young man, “Where did you go?” And he said, “To seek the asses. And when we saw we would not find them, we went to Samuel.”
10:15: And Saul’s uncle said, “Now, tell me what Samuel said to you.”
10:16: And Saul said to his uncle, “He told us plainly that the asses had been found.” But about the matter of the kingdom he did not tell him what Samuel had said.
10:17: Now Samuel gathered the people together before the LORD at Mizpah.
10:18: And he said to the sons of Israel, “Thus said the LORD the God of Israel, ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that were oppressing you.’
10:19: But you have this day despised the worship of your God, the one who saved you from all your evil and your distress, and you have said before Him, ‘We cannot be saved, unless you appoint a king over us.’ Now, take your stand before the LORD by your tribes and by your thousands.”
10:20: Then Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of the House of Benjamin was singled out.
10:21: He brought the tribe of the House of Benjamin near by its families, and the family of Matar was singled out. Then Saul the son of Kish was singled out. But when they sought him, he could not be found.
10:22: So they inquired again of the speech of the LORD “Is the man still here?” And the LORD said, “Behold, he is hidden among the vessels.”
10:23: And they ran and led him from there. And when he stood among the people, he was taller than all the people from his shoulder upward.
10:24: And Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see whom the LORD has chosen? For there is none like him among all the people.” And all the people shouted, “May the king prosper!”
10:25: Then Samuel discussed the royal rights with the people, and he wrote them in a book and deposited it before the LORD Then Samuel sent all the people away, each to his home.
10:26: And also Saul went to his home at The Hill, and with him went part of the people, men fearing sin, in whose hearts fear from before the LORD was given.
10:27: But evil men said, “How can this one save us?” And they despised him and did not ask about his well being. But he was like one who is silent.
11:1: And Nahash, the king of the sons of Ammon, went up and besieged Jabesh gilead; and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.”
11:2: And Nahash, the king of the sons of Ammon, said to them, “If you do this, I will make a treaty with you in that I gouge out all your right eyes and I put disgrace upon all Israel.”
11:3: The elders of Jabesh said to him, “Wait for us for seven days that we may send messengers through all the territory of the land of Israel. Then, if there is no one to save us, we will come out to you.”
11:4: When the messengers came to The Hill of Saul, they spoke the words before thepeople; and all the people lifted up their voice and wept.
11:5: Now Saul was coming from the field behind the oxen; and Saul said, “What ails the people, that they are weeping?” So they told him the words of the men of Jabesh.
11:6: And a mighty spirit from before the LORD dwelt upon Saul, when he heard these words, and his anger was very strong.
11:7: And he took the yoke of oxen and cut them in pieces and sent them throughout allthe territory of Israel by the hand of messengers, saying, “Whoever does not come out after Saul and after Samuel, so shall it be done to his ox!” Then the dread from before the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out as one man.
11:8: When he counted them at Bezek, the men of Israel were three hundred thousand and the men of Judah thirty thousand.
11:9: And they said to the messengers who had come, “Thus shall you say to the men of Jabesh gilead, ‘Tomorrow, about the heat of the day, you shall experience salvation.’” When the messengers came and told the men of Jabesh, they rejoiced.
11:10: And the men of Jabesh said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do to us whatever seems right in your sight.”
